title: Cranberries for preventing urinary tract infections
prompt:
What is the effect of cranberry products (juice, capsules, tablets or powder, at any dose) compared with placebo, no treatment or a non-active control on the occurrence of symptomatic, culture-verified urinary tract infection (UTI) in women with recurrent UTIs?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) using a random-effects model. RR < 1 means fewer women with a UTI in the cranberry arm (favours cranberry).

Outcome: number of participants with at least one symptomatic, culture-verified UTI during the study follow-up (events) out of the number of participants analysed in each arm (total).
- Use participants (not episodes). If a paper reports only the number of UTI episodes or an incidence rate, do not convert it into a participant count.
- Use the paper's primary UTI definition that combines symptoms with a positive urine culture. Do not use asymptomatic bacteriuria, bacteriuria alone or a symptoms-only definition when a culture-verified one is reported.
- Use the intention-to-treat sample when it is reported; otherwise use the analysed sample the paper reports. State which was used.
- If a paper reports UTI at several follow-up times, use the total over the whole study period (the longest follow-up on treatment).
- Multi-arm trials: if there are several cranberry arms (different doses, juice versus tablets), combine them into one cranberry group by summing events and participants. Use only the placebo/no-treatment arm as the control group. Ignore arms that test a different active agent (e.g. probiotics, antibiotics) and do not count them as controls.
- Include women with a history of recurrent UTIs (e.g. two or more episodes in a year or three or more in two years), including both currently infected and infection-free women at baseline. Exclude trials in children, pregnant women, older people in institutions, or people with neurogenic bladder or catheters.

Do not pool UTI outcomes that are asymptomatic bacteriuria, adverse effects, adherence, dropouts, urinary E. coli counts or antibiotic use. Include only randomised controlled trials; exclude cranberry-versus-antibiotic or cranberry-versus-probiotic comparisons with no placebo/no-treatment arm.

title: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder
prompt:
What is the effect of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs: sertraline, fluoxetine, paroxetine, escitalopram, citalopram or similar), given continuously, in the luteal phase only, or at symptom onset, compared with placebo, on self-rated overall premenstrual symptoms in women with premenstrual syndrome or premenstrual dysphoric disorder?

Effect measure: pool as a standardised mean difference (SMD, Hedges' g) using a random-effects model. SMD < 0 means fewer premenstrual symptoms with the SSRI (favours the SSRI).

Outcome: the woman's own overall rating of premenstrual symptoms, extracted as the end-of-treatment mean, SD and number of women per arm.
- Use one self-rated overall symptom measure per trial, such as a daily symptom diary total (for example the Daily Record of Severity of Problems, Daily Symptom Rating Form, Penn Daily Symptom Report, or a Calendar of Premenstrual Experiences total), a visual analogue scale total, or the Patient Global Evaluation. Do not use clinician-rated scales (for example Hamilton or Montgomery-Asberg depression scores, or the Clinical Global Impression).
- Orient every scale so that a higher score means more symptoms; reverse the sign of any scale where a higher score means improvement, so that negative values favour the SSRI.
- Use the end-of-treatment value from the last treatment cycle (or the cycle the paper reports as primary). If only a change from baseline is reported, use the mean change and SD of change for both arms and state it. Do not mix an end value in one arm with a change score in the other.
- If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n.
- Multi-arm trials (several SSRI doses, or continuous and luteal dosing against one placebo group): give each SSRI arm its own comparison against the placebo group, and split the placebo group's n equally across them so placebo women are not counted twice.
- Cross-over trials: use the first-period data if reported; otherwise use the reported means and SDs and state it.
- Include only randomised placebo-controlled trials in women with premenstrual syndrome or PMDD (diagnosed by DSM or equivalent criteria). Exclude trials of non-SSRI antidepressants, herbal or calcium treatments given as the main comparison, and trials without a placebo arm. If a trial compares an SSRI with an herbal or other treatment and with placebo, use only the SSRI arm and the placebo arm.

Do not pool clinician-rated outcomes, physical symptoms alone, adverse events, dropouts, or functional impairment.

title: Galantamine for dementia due to Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment
prompt: What is the effect of galantamine 16 to 24 mg/day (8 to 12 mg twice daily), compared with placebo, on cognitive function (ADAS-cog change from baseline at 6 months) in people with Alzheimer's disease?  This is specifically the 16-24 mg/day (regular release) dose arm — not the 8 mg/day, the prolonged-release 16-24 mg/day, or the 32 mg/day arms, which are separate dose subgroups in this review. Two of the trials here (Tariot 2000, Brodaty 2005) tested multiple galantamine doses against one shared placebo group — extract only this specific dose arm's data against that shared placebo, not the other dose arm from the same trial.  Pool as a Mean Difference (MD), since all studies use the same ADAS-cog instrument.

title: Interventions for smoking cessation in hospitalised patients
cochrane_topic: Lifestyle and wellbeing behaviour and conditions
prompt:
What is the effect of bupropion, compared with placebo or no bupropion, on smoking cessation at the longest follow-up of at least six months in adults who smoke and are hospitalised (for any reason, including cardiovascular admissions)?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) of being abstinent from smoking, bupropion divided by control, using a random-effects model. RR > 1 means more people quit smoking with bupropion (favours bupropion).

Outcome: the number of participants abstinent from smoking (events) out of the number randomised to each arm (total), at the longest follow-up of six months or more.
- Use the longest follow-up reported that is at least six months (for example 6 or 12 months). Do not use 3-month or earlier results.
- Use the strictest abstinence definition each trial reports: prefer sustained or continuous abstinence, biochemically validated where available; otherwise use point-prevalence abstinence, and state which definition was used. Do not use self-reported "reduced smoking".
- Count everyone randomised in the denominator and treat participants lost to follow-up as still smoking (the standard intention-to-treat rule for smoking trials). If a paper gives the quit rate as a percentage, convert it to a count with the number randomised to that arm.
- If a paper reports only the number analysed in a table, use the randomised numbers from the participant-flow diagram when available, and say which numbers you used.
- Control: placebo or no bupropion (usual care). Exclude trials whose control group receives another smoking-cessation drug (nicotine replacement or varenicline).
- Multi-arm trials: include the bupropion arm and the control arm only; if bupropion is combined with counselling in both arms, compare the arms that differ only by bupropion.
- Assign arms by treatment, not by column position.
- Include only randomised controlled trials in hospitalised adult smokers. Exclude trials in outpatients and trials of non-drug interventions.

Do not pool short-term quitting, adverse events, cardiovascular events, withdrawal symptoms or any other outcome.

title: Conservative, physical and surgical interventions for managing faecal incontinence and constipation in adults with central neurological diseases
prompt:
What is the effect of probiotics, compared with no active treatment, placebo, or usual
care, on self-reported improvement in constipation (proportion of participants improved)?

This is specifically the PROBIOTICS subgroup — do not include the "assessment-based nursing
intervention" subgroup, a different conservative intervention type in this same analysis.

Pool as a Risk Ratio (RR) using each trial's reported number of participants with
self-reported improvement and total randomized per arm.

title: Non-corticosteroid immunosuppressive medications for steroidsensitive nephrotic syndrome in children
prompt: What is the effect of rituximab compared with tacrolimus on relapse by 12 months in children with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome? Pool as a Risk Ratio (RR) using each trial's reported relapse events and total randomized per arm.

title: Surgical approach to hysterectomy for benign gynaecological disease
prompt:
What is the effect of laparoscopic hysterectomy (laparoscopically assisted vaginal hysterectomy, total laparoscopic hysterectomy, or laparoscopic hysterectomy of unspecified type), compared with vaginal hysterectomy, on the need for blood transfusion in women undergoing hysterectomy for benign gynaecological disease?

Effect measure: pool as an odds ratio (OR) using a fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel model if available, otherwise random effects. OR > 1 means more transfusions with laparoscopic hysterectomy.

Outcome: number of women who received a blood transfusion (events) out of the number randomised to each arm (total), during the operation and the hospital stay or up to the end of follow-up.
- Use any transfusion (intra-operative or post-operative). Do not use blood loss volume, haemoglobin drop or haematoma.
- If a trial has no transfusions in either arm, record zero events with the arm sizes and keep the row visible; it carries no weight in the odds ratio.
- Compute the OR from the event counts (laparoscopic as the treatment group, vaginal hysterectomy as the control). Assign arms by procedure description, not by column position.
- Multi-arm trials: when a trial compares more than one laparoscopic approach (for example laparoscopically assisted vaginal and total laparoscopic hysterectomy) with the same vaginal hysterectomy group, include each laparoscopic approach as its own comparison and split the vaginal hysterectomy group's size and events equally among them so those women are not counted twice. Ignore arms with abdominal hysterectomy or robotic hysterectomy.
- Use the number randomised as the denominator (intention-to-treat).
- Include only randomised controlled trials comparing a laparoscopic approach with vaginal hysterectomy in women with benign disease. Exclude comparisons with abdominal or robotic hysterectomy, studies of malignancy, and non-randomised studies.

Do not pool operating time, hospital stay, complications other than transfusion, return to normal activities, conversion to laparotomy, pain or cost.

title: Exercise for osteoarthritis of the knee
prompt: What is the effect of exercise, compared with no treatment, usual care, or limited education, on quality of life at 12-month follow-up (sustainability of effect) in adults with knee osteoarthritis?  This is specifically the LONGER-TERM follow-up (up to and including 12 months post-intervention) — do not include quality-of-life data measured immediately at the end of the intervention period; that is a separate, earlier timepoint in this review.  The comparator is no treatment, usual care, or limited/minimal education — NOT an attention-control/placebo condition, and NOT a co-intervention comparison (i.e. do not include trials where exercise was added on top of another treatment and compared to that treatment alone — those are two separate comparisons in this review).  For quality of life, each study may report several outcome measures — identify whichever specific instrument the paper itself frames as its quality-of-life outcome (check its own methods/outcomes description), rather than defaulting to the first similarly-named score in a results table. Pool this as a standardized mean difference, since different studies use different specific instruments/scales for this construct.

title: Magnesium sulphate for women at risk of preterm birth for neuroprotection of the fetus
prompt:
What is the effect of antenatal magnesium sulphate given to women at risk of preterm birth, compared with placebo, on cerebral palsy in their children up to 2 years' corrected age?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) of cerebral palsy, magnesium sulphate divided by placebo, using a fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel model if available, otherwise random effects. RR < 1 means fewer children with cerebral palsy after magnesium (favours magnesium).

Outcome: the number of children with cerebral palsy (events) out of the number of children in each arm who were assessed or counted (total), at the follow-up of about 2 years' corrected age.
- Use the first follow-up at 18 months to 2 years' corrected age that the trial reports. Do not use school-age follow-up.
- Use the trial's own diagnosis of cerebral palsy (for example abnormalities of tone with loss of motor function, or an overall neurological diagnosis made by a paediatric assessor), and state it.
- Use the denominator the paper gives for this outcome, which is usually surviving children with an assessment or all live births with data; state which one. If a paper gives both, use the number of children with data on cerebral palsy. If only the number randomised is given, use it and say so.
- Count children, not mothers or pregnancies. For multiple pregnancies, use the number of children the paper counts for this outcome.
- If a paper gives the rate as a percentage only, convert it to a count with the child numbers in that arm.
- If a trial has several magnesium dose regimens, combine them into one magnesium group and use the placebo group once.
- Include only randomised placebo-controlled trials of antenatal magnesium sulphate given for neuroprotection (not for pre-eclampsia or tocolysis). Exclude trials that compare two magnesium regimens or compare magnesium with another drug.

Do not pool death, death or cerebral palsy combined, substantial gross motor dysfunction, blindness, deafness, maternal outcomes or adverse events.

title: Omega-3 fatty acids for depression in adults
prompt: What is the effect of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFAs: EPA, DHA or a combination, as capsules or supplements), compared with placebo, on quality of life in adults with depression (including major depressive disorder, depressive symptoms, or depression in a medical or neurological condition)?  Pool as a standardised mean difference (SMD, Hedges' g), random effects. SMD < 0 means better quality of life with omega-3 (favours omega-3).  Extract the end-of-treatment mean, SD and n per arm for one quality-of-life measure per trial (prefer the total or overall score). Orient every scale so that a higher score means better quality of life (reverse the sign of scales where a higher score means worse), then compute the SMD so that negative = better with omega-3. If a trial has several omega-3 arms (for example EPA only and EPA+DHA) or several patient groups against one placebo group, give each arm or group its own row and split the placebo group's n equally across them. Convert SE to SD where needed. Use only randomised placebo-controlled trials in adults; do not pool depression severity, response, dropouts or adverse events.

title: Daily oral iron supplementation during pregnancy
prompt:
What is the effect of any iron-containing supplement, compared with the same supplement
without iron or no treatment/placebo, on maternal iron-deficiency anaemia at term (defined
as haemoglobin less than 110 g/L plus at least one additional laboratory indicator of iron
deficiency, assessed at 37 weeks' gestation or later) during pregnancy? If a trial reports
zero events in both arms, treat it as not estimable and exclude it from pooling.

title: Breastfeeding or breast milk for procedural pain in neonates
prompt: What is the effect of breastfeeding (direct breastfeeding or breast milk given during the procedure), compared with no intervention (routine care or no analgesic or comfort measure), on the duration of crying in seconds in term or preterm neonates undergoing a painful procedure (heel lance, venipuncture, intramuscular or intradermal injection, or similar)?  Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in seconds using a random-effects model. MD < 0 means less crying with breastfeeding (favours breastfeeding).  Outcome: duration of crying in seconds, extracted as the mean, SD and number of neonates per arm. - Use the total duration of crying during and immediately after the painful procedure (also called crying time or duration of first cry, as the paper defines it). If a paper reports several crying measures, prefer total crying time over latency to first cry, and do not use pain scores or percentages of time crying. - Convert minutes to seconds. Record the original unit and any conversion. - If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE. If a paper reports only a median and range or interquartile range, estimate the mean and SD with a standard method and state it. - Control = no intervention (routine care, no analgesia, nothing given). Do not use another active control (sucrose, glucose, water, positioning, non-nutritive sucking, skin-to-skin contact without breastfeeding), for which the review has separate comparisons. - Multi-arm trials: when a paper compares breastfeeding, several other interventions and a no-intervention control, extract only the breastfeeding arm and the no-intervention arm. Read the column headings or group definitions carefully, because the no-intervention group may be listed first or last. If the same breastfeeding group appears in several comparisons, it can be used once here against the no-intervention group. - One row per trial; if a trial reports results separately for different procedures, use the primary procedure. - Include only randomised and quasi-randomised controlled trials in neonates (up to 28 days of age). Exclude studies in older infants and studies with no no-intervention arm.  Do not pool heart rate, oxygen saturation, pain scores such as PIPP or NIPS, crying measured as a percentage of time, or any other outcome.

title: Rehabilitation for ankle fractures in adults
prompt:
What is the effect of a removable ankle support, compared with a non-removable ankle
support (e.g. a cast), on activity limitation at end of treatment after surgical fracture
management? Studies use different measurement tools (e.g. OMAS, Mazur score) — pool as a standardized mean difference. A higher score means better activity/function on these
instruments.

title: Haemostatic therapies for stroke due to acute, spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage
prompt:
What is the effect of antifibrinolytic drugs (tranexamic acid, aminocaproic acid or similar), compared with placebo or open (no-drug) control, on intracerebral haematoma expansion by 24 hours in adults with acute spontaneous (non-traumatic) intracerebral haemorrhage?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) using a random-effects model. RR < 1 means fewer patients with haematoma expansion in the antifibrinolytic arm (favours antifibrinolytic).

Outcome: number of participants with haematoma expansion (events) out of the number randomised to each arm (total), assessed on repeat brain imaging at or around 24 hours after the baseline scan.
- Use the paper's own definition of haematoma expansion/growth (typically relative growth of 33% or more, or an absolute increase of about 6 mL or more; other definitions are acceptable if that is what the trial reports). If a paper reports only a mean change in volume and no count of patients with expansion, leave the study out rather than inventing a count.
- Use the number randomised to each arm as the denominator (intention-to-treat), even when percentages in the paper are calculated from the smaller number with a follow-up scan. If a paper reports only a percentage, convert it to a count using the arm size it applies to, and say which denominator was used.
- Use the primary 24-hour scan. Do not use later scans, 7-day or 90-day outcomes.
- Include only patients with spontaneous ICH. If a trial recruited a mixed population (e.g. traumatic and spontaneous haemorrhage), use only the spontaneous-ICH subgroup.
- Multi-arm trials: use the antifibrinolytic arm and the placebo/open-control arm only; combine different antifibrinolytic doses by summing events and participants.
- Be careful with arm order: assign arms by treatment name from the group definitions, not by column position.

Do not pool death or dependence, mortality, serious adverse events, thromboembolic events or functional outcomes. Include only randomised controlled trials; exclude trials of other haemostatic agents (e.g. recombinant factor VIIa, vitamin K, prothrombin complex concentrate, platelet transfusion) and reviews or case series.

title: Interventions for the treatment of oral cavity and oropharyngeal cancers: surgical treatment
prompt: What is the effect of elective (immediate, prophylactic) neck dissection compared with therapeutic (delayed, watchful waiting with dissection on relapse) neck dissection on disease-free survival, defined as the time to new disease, disease progression or death, in adults with early-stage oral cavity (including oral tongue) squamous cell carcinoma and a clinically node-negative neck?  Effect measure: pool as a hazard ratio (HR) using a random-effects model on the log hazard ratio. HR < 1 means longer disease-free survival with elective neck dissection (favours elective).  Outcome: disease-free survival (also called event-free, relapse-free or recurrence-free survival), where events are recurrence or progression or death from any cause, as a hazard ratio with its 95% confidence interval comparing elective with therapeutic neck dissection. - Use the hazard ratio and 95% confidence interval reported in the paper, preferring the intention-to-treat analysis and the longest follow-up. Convert the confidence interval to a standard error of the log HR. - If a paper reports only a hazard ratio for overall survival or for death, do not use it for this outcome; look for the disease-free or event-free survival hazard ratio instead. - If a paper does not report a hazard ratio for disease-free survival but gives a log-rank test with an observed/expected event count, or numbers of events per arm together with a log-rank p-value, estimate the hazard ratio and its variance from those data using the standard indirect methods (Peto's O-E/V or Parmar's methods), and state which method was used. If neither a hazard ratio nor those statistics are reported, leave the study out rather than estimating it. - Orient the HR as elective versus therapeutic, and invert it (HR to 1/HR, with the interval swapped) if the paper reports therapeutic versus elective. - Assign arms by treatment description: elective = neck dissection performed at the time of primary tumour surgery; therapeutic = observation followed by neck dissection only if nodes appear. - Include only randomised controlled trials in adults. Exclude single-arm studies, non-randomised comparisons and trials of radiotherapy or sentinel node biopsy only.  Do not pool overall survival alone, locoregional recurrence, recurrence rates, adverse events or quality of life.

title: Intermittent preventive treatment regimens for malaria in HIVpositive pregnant women
prompt: What is the effect of daily cotrimoxazole (CTXp) combined with another antimalarial drug (mefloquine or dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine), compared with CTXp with or without placebo (current standard of care), on low birth weight (less than 2500 g) in HIV-positive pregnant women? Pool as a Risk Ratio (RR) using each trial's reported low-birth-weight events and total randomized per arm.

title: Conventional versus LigaSure hemorrhoidectomy for patients with symptomatic Hemorrhoids
prompt:
What is the effect of LigaSure haemorrhoidectomy (vessel-sealing device), compared with conventional haemorrhoidectomy (scissors, diathermy or other conventional excision such as Milligan-Morgan or Ferguson), on operating time in minutes in adults with symptomatic haemorrhoids?

Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in minutes using a random-effects model. MD < 0 means a shorter operation with LigaSure (favours LigaSure).

Outcome: operating time (duration of the haemorrhoidectomy operation) in minutes, extracted as the mean, SD and number of patients per arm.
- Use operating time from skin incision (or start of the haemorrhoidectomy) to the end of the procedure, in minutes. Do not use anaesthesia time, total theatre time, or time to haemostasis alone.
- If a paper reports a median with range or interquartile range, estimate the mean and SD with a standard method and state it. If it reports a range only, estimate the SD from the range and state it.
- If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE.
- Convert seconds or hours to minutes. Record the original unit and any conversion.
- Treatment = LigaSure; control = conventional (diathermy, scissors or Ferguson). Assign arms by procedure, not by column position.
- Multi-arm trials: include only LigaSure and a conventional excision arm. Ignore stapled haemorrhoidopexy, laser, Doppler-guided and other arms; if there are two conventional arms, combine them or use the one that matches the review question and state the choice.
- Use the number randomised or analysed as reported.
- Include only randomised controlled trials in adults. Exclude non-randomised comparisons and trials without a conventional-haemorrhoidectomy arm.

Do not pool blood loss, post-operative pain, wound healing, complications, hospital stay, recurrence or return to work.

title: Cerebrolysin for acute ischaemic stroke
prompt:
Meta-analysis of randomised placebo-controlled trials of Cerebrolysin (or Cortexin) in adults with acute ischaemic stroke.

Outcome: all-cause death (mortality from any cause) during the trial follow-up, as the number of participants who died out of the number randomised in each arm. Use the longest follow-up the trial reports for mortality (for example day 90 or the end of the trial).

Effect measure: Risk Ratio (RR), Cerebrolysin or Cortexin versus placebo, using event counts. Values below 1 favour the treatment group.

Outcome rules:
- Treatment arm = Cerebrolysin (or Cortexin) as an add-on or alone. Control arm = placebo (saline). If a trial has several treatment dose groups, add the events and the participants across the dose groups and compare them against the single placebo group once, so the placebo participants are not counted twice.
- Use deaths from any cause, including deaths reported in the safety or adverse-events section. Do not use stroke-related deaths only, and do not use functional outcomes (mRS, NIHSS, Barthel).
- Use the randomised group sizes if the analysed Ns are not reported.
- If a trial reports zero deaths in both arms, keep it in the extraction but note it.

Include all trials found in the uploaded papers. Do not exclude a trial because of its dose, its duration, or because it also tested another drug together with Cerebrolysin (for example alteplase). Exclude only reviews, protocols and trials without a placebo control.

title: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) versus percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) or retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS) for kidney stones
prompt:
What is the effect of extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL, also called SWL), compared with retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS, flexible ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy), on treatment success at three months in adults with kidney stones?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) of treatment success, ESWL divided by RIRS, using a random-effects model. RR < 1 means a lower success rate with ESWL (favours RIRS).

Outcome: number of participants who were treated successfully (events) out of the number randomised to each arm (total), at the three-month follow-up.
- Treatment success means stone-free, or free of clinically significant residual fragments, at about three months, as imaging (CT, ultrasound or X-ray) defines it in the paper. Use the trial's own definition of success (for example fully stone-free or residual fragments of 4 mm or less) and state it.
- If a trial reports the stone-free rate only at a different time (for example one month or six months), use the closest time to three months and say which. If a trial reports a rate in percent only, convert it to a count using the number analysed in that arm.
- If a paper reports failures (residual stones) instead of successes, convert them to successes (total minus failures).
- Include trials that compared ESWL, RIRS and possibly percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL): extract only the ESWL and RIRS arms, and ignore the PCNL arm. If several RIRS or ESWL sessions are allowed, use the outcome after the full planned treatment course.
- Use the number randomised as the denominator (intention-to-treat). Assign arms by treatment description, not by column position.
- Include only randomised controlled trials in adults with renal (kidney) stones. Exclude ureteral stones, studies of children, and trials that compare ESWL with PCNL only.
- If a source is only a conference abstract, extract what is reported there and state that the data came from an abstract.

Do not pool operating time, hospital stay, complications, re-treatment, pain, stone size reduction or quality of life.

title: Internet-based interventions for smoking cessation
cochrane_topic: Lifestyle and wellbeing behaviour and conditions
prompt: In adult smokers, what is the effect of an Internet-based smoking cessation intervention combined with behavioural support, compared with a non-Internet-based non-active control, on smoking cessation at 6 months or longer follow-up? Evaluate ONLY smoking cessation/abstinence at ≥6 months. Use the study’s most rigorous reported definition of abstinence used for this comparison, and use one endpoint per study. Do not extract, classify, or pool short-term cessation outcomes (<6 months), quit attempts, smoking reduction, nicotine dependence, intervention usage, self-efficacy, or other outcomes. Pool the outcome as a dichotomous effect using Risk Ratio (RR).

title: Calcium supplementation (other than for preventing or treating hypertension) for improving pregnancy and infant outcomes
prompt:
What is the effect of high-dose calcium supplementation, compared with placebo or no
treatment, on preterm birth before 37 weeks' gestation, specifically in the dose-stratified
analysis (high-dose subgroup)? Do not include the non-dose-stratified version of this
outcome or the timing-stratified ("started to take calcium") version — those are separate
analyses in this review. Pool as a Risk Ratio (RR) using each trial's reported preterm
birth events and total randomized per arm. If a trial reports zero events in both arms,
treat it as not estimable and exclude it from pooling.

title: Home-based versus centre-based cardiac rehabilitation
cochrane_topic: Lifestyle and wellbeing behaviour and conditions
prompt: In adults with heart disease, what is the effect of home-based cardiac rehabilitation (including digital/telehealth-supported programmes) versus supervised centre-based cardiac rehabilitation on triglycerides at 3–12 months follow-up?  Evaluate ONLY triglycerides. Use the latest eligible follow-up between 3 and 12 months and convert triglyceride values to mmol/L when necessary using a valid universal conversion factor. Extract arm-level mean, SD, and N; either absolute follow-up values or change-from-baseline values are acceptable, whichever the paper reports, and do not exclude a study solely because it reports change scores. If only median/IQR is reported, estimate mean/SD using Wan et al. (2014). For multi-arm trials, extract each eligible home-based intervention vs shared centre-based control comparison separately. Exclude usual-care/waitlist/non-centre comparators, protocols, non-RCTs, and all outcomes other than triglycerides.

title: Cognitive behavioural therapy and third-wave approaches for anxiety and related disorders in older people
prompt: In older adults (≥55 years) with an anxiety or related disorder, what is the effect of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) compared with minimal management on dropout rates at 3–6 months post-treatment?  Evaluate ONLY dropout/discontinuation at 3–6 months post-treatment — not immediate post-treatment dropout. Minimal management may include waiting list, usual care, supportive/attention control, or medication without active psychological therapy; exclude comparisons against another active psychological therapy. Extract dropout events and total participants per arm, and pool using risk ratio (RR).  Dropout counts are often stated in narrative text rather than tables — read Results/Attrition/Sample-Selection sections carefully, not just tables. If a paper reports dropout in two explicitly-stated sequential intervals (e.g., "X by post-treatment, plus Y more by 6 months"), sum them for the cumulative total — this is arithmetic on stated numbers, not an estimate, and should not be left null. If multiple eligible follow-ups fall within the 3–6 month window, use the latest one. Exclude protocols and non-RCTs, and extract no other outcome.

title: HMG CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) for people with chronic kidney disease not requiring dialysis
prompt: What is the effect of statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, e.g. pravastatin, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, fluvastatin, lovastatin, cerivastatin, simvastatin), compared with placebo or no statin treatment (with other treatments given equally to both arms), on proteinuria at the end of treatment in adults with chronic kidney disease not requiring dialysis?  Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in grams per 24 hours (g/24 h) using a random-effects model. MD < 0 means lower proteinuria with statin (favours statin).  Outcome: urinary protein excretion (24-hour urinary protein or, if that is the study's only measure of urinary protein loss, 24-hour urinary albumin excretion) measured at the end of the treatment period. Extract the final (end-of-treatment) mean, SD and number of participants for each arm. - Use end-of-treatment values, not change from baseline and not baseline values. If several follow-up times are reported, use the last on-treatment timepoint (end of the randomised treatment period, before any washout, crossover or withdrawal phase). - Convert all values to g/24 h (e.g. mg/24 h ÷ 1000; mg/day = mg/24 h). Record the original units and the conversion applied. - If variability is reported as SE/SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n for that arm. Check table footnotes and the statistics section for whether "±" is SD or SEM. - If end-of-treatment values appear only in a figure, read the mean and error bar for each arm from the figure, and convert SEM to SD if the error bars are SEM. - Multiple reports of the same trial (same authors, centre, intervention and recruitment period): extract once, from the report with the full randomised sample, and do not add companion or interim reports as separate studies. - Multi-arm trials or trials with a non-CKD control group: use only the CKD participants randomised to statin vs placebo/no statin.  Do not pool kidney function (eGFR, creatinine clearance, serum creatinine), cholesterol/lipid outcomes, cardiovascular events, death, adverse events or urinary podocytes. Exclude people on dialysis or with a kidney transplant, and exclude comparisons of statin vs another statin or vs a different active drug.

title: Interventions for improving coverage of childhood immunisation in low- and middle-income countries
prompt: What is the effect of mobile phone reminders (SMS text messages and/or phone calls, including automated voice calls) sent to parents or caregivers, compared with routine immunisation care without reminders, on receipt of the third dose of DTP-containing vaccine (DTP3 / DPT3 / pentavalent-3 / Penta-3) in children in low- and middle-income countries?  Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) using a random-effects model. RR > 1 means more children received DTP3/Penta-3 in the reminder arm (favours reminders).  Outcome: number of children who received DTP3/Penta-3 (events) out of the number randomised to each arm (total), at the study's main follow-up assessment for that dose (e.g. by 14 weeks, 18 weeks, 6 months or 12 months of age). - Extract raw event counts for each arm. If only percentages are reported, convert them to counts using the number randomised in that arm. - Use crude (unadjusted) counts. Do not use adjusted odds ratios, logistic-regression estimates or cluster-adjusted (GEE) risk ratios when raw counts are available, and do not convert an odds ratio into the result. - Use intention-to-treat denominators (all randomised/enrolled participants per arm), not per-protocol or "children seen at follow-up" subsets, when both are reported. - Use the outcome "received / completed Penta-3 (DTP3)" at the primary follow-up. Do not use "timely receipt within 1 week of the due date" or "received without delay" if overall receipt is also reported. - If a study reports the three pentavalent doses separately, use only the third dose (or "completed all 3 doses"). - Multi-arm trials: use the arm receiving reminders only (SMS/phone call alone) as the treatment group and the no-reminder routine-care arm as the control. Ignore arms that combine reminders with monetary or other incentives, education-only arms and other co-interventions.  Do not pool measles, BCG, OPV, yellow fever, "fully immunised" or "all scheduled vaccines" outcomes, timeliness or delay outcomes, or costs. Include only randomised controlled trials (individual or cluster); exclude non-randomised and controlled before-after studies.

title: Antioxidants for adults with chronic kidney disease
prompt:
What is the effect of antioxidant therapy (including vitamin E and other vitamins, N-acetylcysteine, selenium, and other agents with antioxidant or Nrf2-activating action such as bardoxolone methyl or pentoxifylline), compared with placebo, usual care or no treatment, on cardiovascular death in adults with chronic kidney disease (CKD stages 3 to 5, dialysis, or kidney transplant)?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) using a random-effects model. RR < 1 means fewer cardiovascular deaths with antioxidants (favours antioxidants).

Outcome: number of participants who died from cardiovascular causes (events) out of the number randomised or analysed in each arm (total), over the whole follow-up period.
- Use the cardiovascular-death component only. If a study reports a composite endpoint (e.g. cardiovascular events, MI + stroke + cardiovascular death), do not use the composite; look for the cardiovascular-death count among its components or secondary outcomes.
- If the paper lists fatal myocardial infarction, fatal stroke and sudden death separately without a total, sum them only if the paper itself defines them as cardiovascular death.
- If a study reports all-cause deaths and does not report the cause, do not treat all-cause death as cardiovascular death.
- If a paper reports a subgroup of a larger trial that includes participants with CKD, use the CKD subgroup's counts and denominators, not the whole trial's.
- If the number of cardiovascular deaths is not reported in the paper, do not estimate it; leave the study out.
- Multi-arm trials: use the antioxidant arm(s) and the placebo/usual-care arm. If several antioxidant doses are tested, combine them by summing events and participants.

Do not pool all-cause mortality, non-fatal cardiovascular events, composite cardiovascular endpoints, inflammation or oxidative-stress markers, kidney function outcomes or adverse events. Include only randomised controlled trials in adults with CKD; exclude trials in people without kidney disease and comparisons of one antioxidant against another.

title: Pharmacological interventions for pruritus in adult palliative care patients
prompt:
What is the effect of a kappa-opioid agonist (e.g. difelikefalin, nalbuphine, or
nalfurafine), compared with placebo, on pruritus severity (VAS scale, 0-10 cm) in
participants with uremic pruritus, from parallel-group design studies? Pool all
kappa-opioid agonist drugs together as one class rather than separate subgroups per drug.
Do not include crossover-design studies or the fixed-effects sensitivity analysis — those
are separate analyses in this review. Pool as a Mean Difference (MD), since all studies use
the same 0-10 cm VAS pruritus scale. A lower score means less pruritus (better outcome).

title: Interventions for increasing fruit and vegetable consumption in children aged five years and under
cochrane_topic: Lifestyle and wellbeing behaviour and conditions
prompt:
What is the effect of a child-feeding intervention, compared with no-intervention control,
on children's vegetable intake, measured short-term (less than 12 months after the
intervention)? Pool as a standardized mean difference, since studies use different vegetable
intake measures. Do not include longer-term follow-up data — that is a separate outcome in
this review.

title: Single-incision sling operations for urinary incontinence in women
prompt: What is the effect of single-incision mid-urethral slings (SIS; any commercial device except TVT-Secur, e.g. Ajust, Needleless/Contasure, MiniArc, Ophira, Altis, Solyx) compared with transobturator mid-urethral slings (TOT/TVT-O, inside-out or outside-in) on subjective cure or improvement of stress urinary incontinence at 12 months in women undergoing surgery for stress or stress-predominant urinary incontinence?  Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) of the proportion cured or improved, SIS divided by TOT. RR > 1 means more women cured or improved with the single-incision sling.  Outcome: number of women reporting subjective cure or improvement of incontinence (events) out of the number analysed in each arm (total), at the 12-month follow-up. - Use the patient-reported cure/improvement definition the paper gives (e.g. no stress leakage by questionnaire, "very much" or "much improved" on a global impression scale, or satisfaction-based success). Do not use objective cure (cough stress test, pad test, urodynamics). - Use the 12-month assessment. If the paper is a longer follow-up report (24 or 36 months), read the 12-month figures from its tables or figures; do not use the longest follow-up. If 12 months is not reported, use the closest earlier assessment of at least 6 months. - Be careful with arm labels. In some papers the single-incision arm is listed first, in others second. Assign arms by the device description (single-incision / mini-sling vs transobturator tape), not by column position, and keep SIS as the treatment group in every study. - Trials with more than one single-incision arm: report each eligible single-incision arm separately against the shared TOT group, and divide the TOT group's size and events equally across the comparisons so the same women are not counted twice. - Trials that also include a TVT-Secur arm: ignore the TVT-Secur arm and keep any other single-incision arm. - Multiple reports of the same trial: extract once, and prefer the report that gives the 12-month subjective result.  Do not pool objective cure, quality-of-life scores, complications, operating time, pain, reoperation or the 12-to-24-month outcome. Exclude trials that include only TVT-Secur, trials comparing a sling with colposuspension, bulking agents or retropubic slings, and trials with no TOT arm.

title: Memory rehabilitation for people with multiple sclerosis
prompt: In people with multiple sclerosis, what is the effect of memory rehabilitation (compared with a control condition — no intervention, usual care, or an active comparator) on subjective memory (self-reported memory functioning, e.g. via a memory questionnaire) at the intermediate follow-up timepoint (approximately 1 to 6 months after treatment)? Evaluate ONLY subjective memory. Do not extract, classify, or pool any other outcome such as verbal memory, visual memory, working memory, information processing, quality of life, or activities of daily living.

title: Probiotics for the prevention or treatment of chemotherapy- or radiotherapy-related diarrhoea in people with cancer
prompt: What is the effect of probiotics, compared with placebo, on the incidence of grade 2 or higher diarrhoea in people with cancer receiving radiotherapy (with or without chemotherapy)?

title: Vaccines for preventing herpes zoster in older adults
prompt:
What is the effect of live attenuated herpes zoster vaccine (Oka/Merck zoster vaccine, Zostavax), compared with placebo, on the occurrence of adverse events in adults aged 50 years or older?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) using a random-effects model. RR > 1 means more participants had an adverse event with the vaccine.

Outcome: number of participants who had one or more adverse events of any type (injection-site or systemic, vaccine-related or not) during the post-vaccination safety follow-up (events) out of the number randomised or vaccinated in each arm (total).
- Use the outcome "one or more adverse events" (any adverse event). Do not use vaccine-related adverse events, injection-site events alone, systemic events alone, serious adverse events, hospitalisations or death.
- If a trial reports adverse events for a safety substudy of a larger trial, use the substudy counts and denominators for this outcome, and do not use counts for the whole trial where the outcome was not measured in everyone.
- Use the short-term safety follow-up as defined in each paper (for example days 0 to 28 or 0 to 42 after vaccination). If a paper reports several time windows, use the one that covers all adverse events collected after vaccination, not a 3-year follow-up.
- Use the number randomised to each arm as the denominator when the paper gives it, even when the paper's own percentages are calculated on a smaller group with complete safety data. If percentages only are given, convert to counts using the arm size they refer to.
- Arms: assign vaccine vs placebo by group definition; do not use arms that received a different vaccine or a different schedule.
- If a trial has several vaccine batches or doses, combine them into one vaccine group (sum events and participants).
- Include only randomised placebo-controlled trials of the live zoster vaccine. Exclude trials of the recombinant (non-live) zoster vaccine, trials comparing two vaccines, and reviews.

Do not pool vaccine efficacy against herpes zoster, post-herpetic neuralgia, immunogenicity, or any other outcome.

title: Medication review in hospitalised patients to reduce morbidity and mortality
prompt: In hospitalised adult patients, what is the effect of medication review compared with standard care on all-cause mortality at the longest available follow-up? Evaluate ONLY all-cause mortality. Do not extract, classify, or pool other outcomes such as hospital readmissions, emergency department contacts, adverse drug events, or health-related quality of life. Focus only on medication review versus standard care, not comparisons between different types of medication review.

title: Comparisons of approaches to pelvic floor muscle training for urinary incontinence in women
prompt: What is the effect of indirect training (exercises that are NOT pelvic floor muscle contractions, e.g. general core, hip, or trunk exercises) COMBINED WITH direct pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), compared with direct PFMT alone, on incontinence-related quality of life in women with urinary incontinence?  The treatment arm must include BOTH indirect training AND direct PFMT together — not indirect training alone (that is a different comparison in this same review). The control arm is direct PFMT alone, with no added indirect component.  Do not include studies comparing indirect training ALONE (with no PFMT) to direct PFMT, and do not include studies comparing co-ordinated training (body movements performed WITH simultaneous pelvic floor muscle contraction) to direct PFMT — both are separate comparisons in this review, using the same "direct PFMT" comparator but a different treatment arm.  This is the single target outcome — do not pool other outcomes (incontinence episodes, subjective cure/improvement, satisfaction).

title: Collaborative care approaches for people with severe mental illness
prompt:
Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of collaborative care versus usual care in adults with severe mental illness (bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder or other psychotic disorders) treated in community or outpatient settings.

Outcome: health-related quality of life in the MENTAL HEALTH domain, measured as an endpoint score (post-intervention mean and SD per group, not change from baseline), at the follow-up closest to 6 months and no later than 6 months.

Effect measure: Standardised Mean Difference (SMD, Hedges' g), collaborative care minus usual care. Different scales are used, so standardise. Positive values favour collaborative care (higher score = better quality of life).

Outcome rules:
- Use one mental-health quality-of-life score per trial:
  - SF-12 or SF-36 Mental Component Summary (MCS), or
  - the WHOQOL-BREF psychological domain.
- Do not use the physical-health component or the physical domain.
- Do not use the overall or total quality-of-life score.
- Do not use symptom scales, functioning scales or satisfaction scales.
- If a trial reports several follow-ups, use the one at 6 months, or the nearest earlier one if there is none at 6 months (for example 2 months). Do not use 12-month or longer follow-ups.
- Use the randomised group sizes if the analysed Ns are not reported.
- If only SE or a 95% CI is given, convert it to SD using the group n.

Include the trials found in the uploaded papers. Do not exclude a trial because of its diagnosis, its country, or its quality-of-life instrument. Exclude only reviews and protocols, and trials without a usual-care control.

title: Fortification of condiments and seasonings with iron for preventing anaemia and improving health
prompt: What is the effect of iron-fortified condiments or seasonings (for example fortified soy sauce, fish sauce, curry powder, salt or other condiments), compared with the same condiment without added iron, on serum or plasma ferritin concentration in children and adults?  Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in micrograms per litre (µg/L, equal to ng/mL) using a random-effects model. MD > 0 means higher ferritin with the fortified condiment (favours fortification).  Outcome: serum or plasma ferritin concentration at the end of the intervention, extracted as the mean, SD and number of participants per arm. - Use the end-of-intervention value (mean and SD). If a trial reports only the change in ferritin from baseline (mean change and SD of change), use those for both arms and record that change scores were used. Do not mix an end value in one arm with a change score in the other. - If a trial reports several follow-up times, use the last one. - Convert all values to µg/L (for example pmol/L × 0.445 for ferritin). Record the original unit and any conversion. - If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE. - If ferritin is reported as geometric mean with a confidence interval or on a log scale, use the arithmetic mean and SD where the paper gives them; otherwise record the geometric mean and say so. - Cluster-randomised trials (randomised by village, school, household or family): adjust the sample sizes for clustering by dividing both arms' sample sizes by the design effect, 1 + (average cluster size − 1) × ICC, using the ICC reported in the paper. If no ICC is reported, say so and use the paper's own cluster-adjusted analysis if it has one. - Control: the same condiment without added iron. Exclude trials whose control group received iron supplements or a different fortified food. - Multi-arm trials: include the fortified-condiment arm and the unfortified-condiment arm only. Ignore arms with other interventions (for example iron tablets or nutrition education), or combine fortified arms if more than one. - Include only randomised or cluster-randomised controlled trials of condiment or seasoning fortification with iron (alone or with other micronutrients added equally to both arms).  Do not pool haemoglobin, anaemia prevalence, iron deficiency, soluble transferrin receptor, body iron, growth or adverse effects.

title: Hormone therapy for sexual function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women
prompt:
What is the effect of estrogen alone (oral, transdermal or vaginal estradiol or conjugated estrogens, at any dose), compared with placebo or no treatment, on sexual function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women?

Effect measure: pool as a standardised mean difference (SMD, Hedges' g) using a random-effects model. SMD > 0 means better sexual function with estrogen (favours estrogen).

Outcome: a composite or overall sexual function score, extracted as the mean, SD and number of women per arm at the end of treatment.
- Use one sexual function measure per trial. Prefer a validated overall sexual function score (for example the Female Sexual Function Index total or full score, the McCoy Female Sexuality Questionnaire total); if only a domain or sub-score of a broader quality-of-life scale is reported (for example the sexual item or domain of the Menopause-Specific Quality of Life questionnaire or the Women's Health Questionnaire), use that.
- Direction: orient every scale so that a higher value means better sexual function. Scales on which a higher score means more bother or a worse symptom (for example the MENQoL sexual domain or symptom bother scores) must have their sign reversed (multiply the means by −1) before computing the SMD.
- Use the end-of-treatment value; if only the change from baseline is reported (mean change and SD of change), use those for both arms and record that change scores were used. Do not mix an end value in one arm with a change score in the other.
- If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n for each arm. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE.
- If a trial reports several time points within the treatment period, use the last one at or before the end of treatment, or combine them only if the paper itself does.
- Control: placebo or no treatment. Exclude trials whose control group receives another hormone, testosterone, DHEA, tibolone or a vaginal moisturizer.
- Multi-arm trials: include the estrogen-alone arm and the placebo arm only; combine several estrogen doses into one group (pool means and SDs, sum participants). Ignore arms combining estrogen with progestogen or testosterone.
- Include only randomised placebo-controlled trials in peri- or postmenopausal women. Exclude trials in premenopausal women or after cancer treatment.

Do not pool vaginal atrophy symptoms, vasomotor symptoms, bone, endometrial or adverse-effect outcomes, or sexual function measured only at follow-up after stopping treatment.

title: Androgens (dehydroepiandrosterone or testosterone) for women undergoing assisted reproduction
prompt:
What is the effect of testosterone pretreatment (e.g. transdermal testosterone gel or patch before ovarian stimulation), compared with placebo or no treatment, on live birth or ongoing pregnancy in women undergoing assisted reproduction (IVF or ICSI)?

Measurement: number of women with a live birth per woman randomised; where live birth is not reported, use ongoing pregnancy. Analyse as a dichotomous outcome (odds ratio). If a trial has several testosterone-duration arms, compare each arm with the control group split equally among them. Do not pool clinical pregnancy, miscarriage, multiple pregnancy, oocyte numbers, adverse effects or any other outcome, and do not include DHEA trials or comparisons against other active interventions.

title: Interventions for preventing the progression of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
prompt: What is the effect of vasopressin type 2 receptor (V2R) antagonists compared with control (placebo or standard therapy) on serious adverse events in people with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease? Pool as a Risk Ratio (RR) using each trial's reported serious adverse event counts and total randomized per arm.

title: Exercise for treating patellofemoral pain syndrome
prompt: What is the effect of exercise therapy, compared with control (no treatment, placebo, waiting list or health educational material, including exercise plus a co-intervention versus that co-intervention alone), on functional ability in the short term (up to 3 months) in people with patellofemoral pain syndrome? Functional ability should be measured with knee-function questionnaires (e.g. Anterior Knee Pain Scale/Kujala, FIQ, WOMAC, Lysholm), preferring the AKPS/Kujala when a study reports more than one.

title: Remote and web 2.0 interventions for promoting physical activity
cochrane_topic: Lifestyle and wellbeing behaviour and conditions
prompt: In adults, what is the effect of remote or web 2.0 physical activity interventions compared with placebo, no intervention, or minimal intervention on self-reported physical activity, measured at 12 months follow-up?  Extract only self-reported physical activity at the 12-month timepoint — exclude cardiorespiratory fitness, dichotomous outcomes (e.g., meeting activity guidelines), and any 24-month follow-up data. Extract raw arm-level mean, SD, and N for each group; different studies may use different physical activity measures/units, so pool as a standardized mean difference (SMD) rather than assuming a common unit. If multiple eligible assessments are reported, use the one closest to 12 months. Exclude protocols and non-RCTs.

title: Intranasal corticosteroids for non-allergic rhinitis
prompt: In adults and adolescents (≥12 years) with non-allergic rhinitis, what is the effect of intranasal corticosteroids compared with placebo on the risk of epistaxis (nosebleed), measured at any point during treatment or follow-up? Extract only epistaxis as a dichotomous adverse event (number of participants experiencing epistaxis and total participants per arm). Include epistaxis whether actively assessed, spontaneously reported, or recorded in a diary/questionnaire. Pool using risk difference (RD). For multi-dose trials, use an intranasal corticosteroid dose within 200–400 µg/day and avoid double-counting a shared placebo group. Exclude other adverse events, nasal symptom scores, quality of life, and airflow outcomes. Exclude protocols and non-RCTs.

title: Belimumab for systemic lupus erythematosus
prompt: In adults with active systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), what is the effect of belimumab at the standard approved dose compared with placebo on achieving at least a 4-point reduction in SELENA-SLEDAI score at 52 weeks?  Extract only the dichotomous ≥4-point reduction in SELENA-SLEDAI at 52 weeks (number of participants achieving the reduction and total participants per arm). For multi-dose trials, use only the belimumab 10 mg/kg arm versus placebo; also include the equivalent approved 200 mg subcutaneous dose when that is the trial's belimumab regimen. Pool using risk ratio (RR). Do not substitute the overall SLE Responder Index (SRI), continuous SELENA-SLEDAI change scores, BILAG, physician global assessment, quality of life, glucocorticoid reduction, adverse events, infections, withdrawals, or mortality. Exclude protocols and non-RCTs.

title: Fibrin-based haemostatic agents for reducing blood loss in adult liver resection
prompt:
What is the effect of fibrin-based haemostatic agents (fibrin sealant, fibrin glue, fibrin patches or fibrin-coated collagen), compared with other haemostatic agents or techniques that are not fibrin-based (for example oxidised cellulose, collagen sponges, argon beam coagulation, electrocautery, or standard surgical haemostasis), on perioperative mortality in adults undergoing liver resection?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) of death, fibrin-based agent divided by the non-fibrin comparator, using a random-effects model. RR > 1 means more deaths with the fibrin-based agent.

Outcome: number of participants who died during the perioperative period (events) out of the number randomised to each arm (total). Perioperative means in hospital or within about 30 to 90 days of the operation, as each paper defines it.
- Count deaths from any cause. Do not use treatment-related deaths only, and do not use late mortality at one year or more.
- If a paper reports that no deaths occurred in an arm, record zero events with the arm size; if it does not report mortality at all, leave the trial out.
- Use the number randomised as the denominator (intention-to-treat). If the paper reports the number in the safety or treated population only, use that and state it.
- Multi-arm trials: include the fibrin-based arm and one non-fibrin comparator arm. If a trial has two non-fibrin arms, combine them into one control group (sum events and participants).
- Assign arms by treatment description, not by column position.
- Include only randomised controlled trials in adults undergoing liver (hepatic) resection. Exclude trials comparing a fibrin agent with no haemostatic agent at all (they belong to a different comparison), comparisons of two fibrin agents, and non-randomised studies.

Do not pool blood loss, time to haemostasis, transfusion, bile leak, reoperation, infection or any other outcome.

title: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy for advanced pancreatic cancer
prompt: What is the effect of a fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy combination, compared with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel, on overall survival in adults with advanced pancreatic cancer?  This is specifically the comparison: fluoropyrimidine-based combination regimens (e.g. regimens combining nab-paclitaxel or gemcitabine with a fluoropyrimidine such as S-1, capecitabine, or 5-FU/leucovorin) versus gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel as the comparator. Do NOT include trials comparing different DOSES or dosing schedules of gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel against each other — that is a separate comparison in this review. Do NOT include any other comparator (e.g. best supportive care, gemcitabine alone, or fluoropyrimidine alone) — those are also separate comparisons in this review, each with their own "overall survival" outcome.  The single target outcome is OVERALL SURVIVAL — not progression-free survival, response rate, or any grade 3/4 adverse event outcome.  Please extract the Risk Ratio (RR) directly from each paper's own Cox proportional hazards / time-to-event survival analysis (log[HR] and its SE, or RR with its 95% CI) — do not approximate a hazard ratio from response-rate or adverse-event counts; if a paper does not report a Cox-model RR for overall survival, treat it as not usable for this outcome rather than substituting a different statistic.

title: Interventions for tobacco use cessation in people living with HIV
prompt:
What is the effect of behavioural support, compared with brief advice or no intervention,
on tobacco use cessation? Keep the three intervention-combination subgroups (behavioural
support alone; behavioural support + NRT; behavioural support + varenicline) as separate
subgroups within one pooled analysis, since each has its own matched control arm (brief
advice, or brief advice + NRT, or varenicline alone respectively).

Some trials tested more than one behavioural-support variant against a single shared
control group — extract each variant as its own row against a proportional share of that
same control group, rather than picking only one variant or discarding the other.

title: Higher blood pressure targets for hypertension in older adults
prompt: What is the effect of a HIGHER blood pressure target (systolic/diastolic approximately 150-160/95-100 mmHg) compared with a LOWER blood pressure target (approximately 140/90 mmHg) on all-cause mortality in older adults with hypertension? The "higher BP target" arm is the treatment/intervention arm, and the "lower BP target" arm is the control/comparator arm — match this exact framing to whichever arm each trial itself labels as its higher vs lower treatment-target group; do not assume "higher target" means "more/stronger treatment," since it is actually the LESS intensively treated arm in these trials. The single target outcome is ALL-CAUSE MORTALITY (death from any cause) — not cardiovascular mortality, non-cardiovascular mortality, stroke, or any other outcome in this review, which are separate analyses. This is dichotomous (event/no-event) data — please pool it as a Risk Ratio (RR), matching how this outcome is conventionally analyzed in this literature, using each trial's reported number of deaths and total randomized per arm.

title: Interventions with pregnant women, new mothers and other primary caregivers for preventing early childhood caries
prompt:
What is the effect of oral hygiene, diet and feeding-practice advice delivered to pregnant women, new mothers or other primary caregivers (for example motivational interviewing, family-centred health promotion, brushing and diet counselling, or photograph-based feedback), compared with standard care or no advice, on the presence of dental caries (tooth decay) in the primary teeth of their children?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) of the child having caries, advice divided by standard care, using a random-effects model. RR < 1 means fewer children with caries with the advice (favours the advice).

Outcome: the number of children with caries in any primary teeth (events) out of the number of children in each arm (total), at the longest follow-up reported.
- Use the trial's own caries definition (for example any decay in the primary teeth, dmfs or dmft above zero, cavitated lesions, decay into dentin, or white-spot lesions) and state which definition was used. Prefer the definition that counts any carious lesion in any primary tooth; do not use only a subset of teeth (for example only the upper front teeth) in this analysis.
- Count children with caries, not the number of teeth or surfaces affected. If a paper reports only mean dmft or dmfs scores, leave it out of this outcome.
- If a paper reports the proportion of children with caries as a percentage, convert it to a count using the number of children assessed in that arm.
- Use the number of children assessed at the follow-up; if only the number randomised is given for that outcome, use it and say so.
- If a trial reports several follow-up times, use the longest one.
- If a trial has several intervention arms, combine those delivering oral hygiene, diet or feeding advice into one group and use the control group once. If an arm adds fluoride or another treatment, use only the advice-only arm.
- Include randomised controlled trials, including cluster-randomised trials; if a cluster trial gives an adjusted risk ratio or odds ratio, use it as reported. Exclude trials of fluoride varnish or xylitol only, and trials with no comparison group.

Do not pool caries severity (dmft or dmfs scores), caries at the front four teeth only, bacterial counts, behaviour or knowledge outcomes, or adverse events.

title: Metformin for endometrial hyperplasia
prompt:
Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials in women with endometrial hyperplasia (with or without atypia) comparing metformin plus megestrol (megestrol acetate) with megestrol alone.

Outcome: regression of endometrial hyperplasia, i.e. the number of women whose endometrium returned to proliferative, secretory or atrophic (normal) endometrium on histology at the end of treatment, out of the number randomised/analysed in each arm.

Effect measure: Odds Ratio (OR), metformin + megestrol versus megestrol alone, using event counts. Events are women WITH regression, so an OR above 1 favours metformin + megestrol.

Outcome rules:
- Treatment arm = metformin + megestrol. Control arm = megestrol alone. Ignore any arm that is metformin alone, a placebo, LNG-IUS or any other treatment.
- Use the histological response at the end of the treatment course (about 3 to 6 months).
- Count complete regression to normal endometrium as the event. Do not count persistence, progression or partial response as events.
- If a trial reports hyperplasia with and without atypia separately, add the counts across both groups.
- If a paper reports only percentages, convert them to counts using the arm sizes.
- Use the randomised group sizes if the analysed Ns are not reported.

Include the trials found in the uploaded papers. Do not exclude a trial because of its dose, its treatment duration or whether atypia was present. Exclude only reviews and protocols, and trials without a megestrol-alone control arm.

title: Interventions for the uptake of evidence-based recommendations in acute stroke settings
prompt: What is the effect of multifaceted implementation interventions (for example education, audit and feedback, local champions, protocols or clinical pathways, with or without changes to how care is delivered), compared with no implementation intervention or usual practice, on adherence to evidence-based recommendations in the care of people with acute stroke during the hospital admission?  Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) of adherence, intervention divided by control, using a random-effects model on the log risk ratio. RR > 1 means higher adherence with the intervention.  Outcome: the proportion of patients (or eligible patients) who received the recommended process of care, extracted as the number adherent (events) out of the number in each arm (total), at the end of the intervention period. - Use the trial's primary adherence or quality-of-care process measure (for example the proportion of eligible patients given thrombolysis, or the proportion receiving a defined care protocol). Do not use patient outcomes such as death, disability or length of stay. - If a trial reports several process measures, use the primary one and report which was used. - Use the numbers of patients, not hospitals or clusters, as events and totals, from the follow-up period after the intervention started (not baseline). If a trial reports a before-and-after comparison, use the post-intervention period only. - Cluster-randomised trials: if the paper reports a cluster-adjusted risk ratio or odds ratio with a confidence interval, use that (convert the interval to a standard error of the log RR; convert an odds ratio to a risk ratio only if the baseline risk is given). Otherwise adjust the standard error by the design effect, 1 + (average cluster size − 1) × ICC, with the ICC reported by the trial or, if none is reported, state an assumed ICC of 0.05. - Control: no intervention, usual care or practice as normal. Exclude trials whose control group receives another implementation strategy. - Multi-arm trials: include only the multifaceted-intervention arm and the control arm; combine several intervention arms into one. - Include only randomised (including cluster-randomised) trials in acute stroke settings. Exclude single-component interventions, studies in other conditions, and uncontrolled before-and-after studies.  Do not pool patient clinical outcomes, costs, staff knowledge or satisfaction, or adherence measured after the hospital admission.

title: Higher versus lower fractions of inspired oxygen or targets of arterial oxygenation for adults admitted to the intensive care unit
prompt:
What is the effect of a higher (liberal) fraction of inspired oxygen or arterial oxygenation target, compared with a lower (conservative) target, on all-cause mortality in adults (aged 18 or over) admitted to the intensive care unit, including patients after cardiac arrest, with acute respiratory failure or ARDS, with septic shock, or receiving mechanical ventilation?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) using a random-effects model. RR > 1 means more deaths with the higher oxygen target.

Outcome: number of participants who died from any cause (events) out of the number randomised to each arm (total), at the longest follow-up reported in the trial (for example 90 days, 180 days or hospital discharge; if only 28 or 30 days is reported, use that).
- Higher oxygen arm = the group assigned the higher or liberal oxygen target or fraction (for example SpO2 above 96%, PaO2 above 13 kPa, or hyperoxia); lower arm = conservative or low-normal target. Assign arms by the target described, not by column position or by which is called "intervention".
- Use the longest follow-up with a death count for all randomised participants. Do not use ICU mortality when a later death count exists.
- Factorial trials: if a trial randomises oxygen and another factor (for example carbon dioxide target, or a drug), compare all participants assigned a higher oxygen target with all assigned a lower oxygen target, summing across the other factor. Do not compare one cell of the factorial with another.
- Use the number randomised as the denominator (intention-to-treat). If a trial reports mortality for fewer participants than were randomised, use all randomised.
- Include only randomised controlled trials of oxygen or oxygenation targets. Exclude trials of hyperbaric oxygen, high-flow nasal oxygen, trials of different devices at the same target, and trials in neonates or children.

Do not pool serious adverse events, ventilator-free days, organ dysfunction scores, neurological outcome, length of stay or intermediate time points such as ICU mortality when a later all-cause mortality count exists.

title: Personalised interventions for subgroups of children with conduct problems
prompt: What is the effect of personalised (tailored or adapted to a subgroup) parenting or family interventions, compared with the standard non-personalised version of the same intervention, on child conduct problems in children with conduct problems, measured on the Eyberg Child Behavior Inventory (ECBI) Problem scale at the end of treatment?  Pool as a mean difference (MD) in ECBI Problem scale points, random effects. MD < 0 favours the personalised intervention.  Extract the post-treatment mean, SD and n per arm for the ECBI Problem scale (not the Intensity scale), from the first assessment after treatment ended. Use the mother's report if several reporters are given. Convert SE to SD where needed. Use only randomised trials in which the control arm is a non-personalised active intervention, not a waitlist or usual care. Do not pool follow-up assessments, the Intensity scale, other behaviour scales or parent outcomes.

title: Fenoldopam for preventing and treating acute kidney injury
prompt:
What is the effect of fenoldopam compared with control (placebo or saline) on development
of acute kidney injury (AKI), across ALL patient populations (not just cardiac surgery
patients — that's a separate subgroup in this review)? Pool as a Risk Ratio (RR) using each
trial's reported AKI events and total randomized per arm.

title: Manual therapy and exercise for lateral elbow pain
prompt: What is the effect of manual therapy (manipulation, mobilisation, soft-tissue techniques), prescribed exercise, or a combination of the two, compared with minimal or no intervention (wait-and-see, advice only, placebo or sham, usual GP care), on pain intensity in adults with lateral elbow pain (tennis elbow, lateral epicondylalgia), measured at the end of the intervention period?  Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) on a 0 to 10 pain scale using a random-effects model. MD < 0 means less pain with the active treatment (favours the treatment). Convert 0 to 100 mm visual analogue scale values to 0 to 10 by dividing means and SDs by 10.  Outcome: mean pain intensity (for example pain at rest, on activity or on maximum grip; prefer the trial's primary pain measure) at the end of the intervention period, extracted as the mean, SD and number of participants per arm. - Use the first assessment at the end of treatment (typically 6 to 8 weeks). Do not use later follow-up assessments. - Use end-of-intervention means and SDs when they are reported. If only the change from baseline is given (mean change and SD of change), use those for both arms and state that change scores were used. If only an adjusted between-group difference with a confidence interval (95% or 99%) is reported, use that: take the SE from the interval (95%: width ÷ 3.92; 99%: width ÷ 5.15) and state that an adjusted difference was used. Do not mix end values and change scores within a trial. - If the number analysed per arm is not stated for the pain outcome, use the number randomised to each arm (or the arm sizes in the flow diagram) and state this. Do not leave group sizes blank. - If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE. - If the paper gives data only in a figure, leave the trial out and say so. - Orient the difference as treatment minus control, and invert it if the paper reports control minus treatment. - A control that receives only advice, stretching, usual care or a placebo or sham counts as minimal intervention. Exclude trials whose control group receives another active manual therapy or exercise programme, or an injection or drug. - Multi-arm trials: include each eligible active arm (manual therapy, exercise, or both) against the shared minimal-intervention group, splitting the control group's n equally across the comparisons; or combine the active arms into one group and use the control once, and state the choice. - Include only randomised controlled trials in adults with lateral elbow pain.  Do not pool disability, grip strength, quality of life, treatment success, withdrawals or adverse events.

title: Mental Health First Aid as a tool for improving mental health and well-being
prompt:
What is the effect of Mental Health First Aid (MHFA) training, compared with a control (waiting list, no training, or an unrelated activity), on trainees' ability to correctly recognise depression in a case vignette at follow-up of six months or longer?

Effect measure: pool as an odds ratio (OR) of correct recognition, MHFA versus control, using a random-effects model on the log odds ratio. OR > 1 means better recognition with training (favours MHFA).

Outcome: the proportion of participants who correctly identified depression in a vignette of a person with depression, at the longest follow-up of at least six months, with the log odds ratio and its standard error.
- Recognition means naming the vignette as depression (or an equivalent diagnostic label such as "major depression") in an open-ended question or a closed choice. Do not use recognition of other disorders (for example schizophrenia or psychosis), knowledge scores, beliefs about treatment or stigma.
