- Use the follow-up of six months or longer. If a trial has several follow-ups (for example 6 and 24 months), use the first one at or after six months. Do not use outcomes measured immediately after training.
- If the paper reports counts or percentages correct in each arm, compute the odds ratio and its standard error from those, using the number analysed in each arm.
- If the paper reports an odds ratio with a 95% confidence interval for recognition, use it as reported (preferably the one adjusted for clustering or baseline) and convert the interval to a standard error of the log OR.
- If the paper reports only a continuous recognition score (for example a mean score out of a maximum on a vignette), convert the standardised mean difference to an odds ratio with the standard formula (log OR = SMD × π/√3), say that this conversion was used, and compute its standard error the same way.
- If the number analysed at follow-up is not clear, use the number randomised and say so.
- Trials with two training groups (for example e-learning and face-to-face, or training with and without a book): combine them into one training group (sum events and participants) and compare with the control once.
- Cluster-randomised trials: use the authors' cluster-adjusted OR if reported; otherwise adjust the standard error by the design effect.
- Include only randomised controlled trials in which participants received MHFA training (including cluster trials). Exclude non-randomised studies and trials without a control group.

Do not pool outcomes other than depression recognition at follow-up, such as stigma, confidence in helping, behaviour towards others, or the effects on people receiving help.

title: Effect of atorvastatin on testosterone levels
prompt: What is the effect of atorvastatin, compared with placebo or no treatment, on withdrawal due to adverse effects in adults?

title: Interventions to prevent surgical site infection in adults undergoing cardiac surgery
prompt: What is the effect of an implantable gentamicin-collagen sponge placed in the sternotomy wound, compared with no topical antimicrobial, on superficial surgical site infection (SSI) in adults undergoing cardiac surgery?  The intervention is specifically a gentamicin-collagen sponge (or gentamicin-impregnated collagen implant) applied locally to the sternal wound during closure — not a general topical antimicrobial, antiseptic wash, or systemic antibiotic.  The single target outcome is SUPERFICIAL surgical site infection — not deep SSI, not mediastinitis, and not the combined/total SSI figure. Deep SSI is a separate, related analysis in this review using the same studies.  This is dichotomous (event/no-event) data — please pool it as a Risk Ratio (RR), using each trial's reported number of superficial SSI events and total randomized per arm.

title: Peripherally inserted central catheter design and material for reducing catheter failure and complications
prompt: What is the effect of peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs) without a valve, compared with PICCs with integrated valve technology (proximal or distal valves), on catheter occlusion in people of any age requiring a PICC? Measurement: number of participants (or catheters) with catheter occlusion during the catheter dwell time, analysed as a dichotomous outcome with the no-valve group as the intervention and the valved group as the comparator. If a trial has more than one valved-catheter arm, combine them. Do not pool catheter failure, venous thromboembolism, infection, breakage or any other outcome, and do not include comparisons of catheter material, tip design or taper alone.

title: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy versus retrograde intrarenal surgery for treatment of renal stones in adults
prompt:
What is the effect of percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL, including mini-, super-mini and micro-PCNL) compared with retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS, flexible ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy) on postoperative pain on the day of surgery (postoperative day 0) in adults with renal stones?

Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in points on a 0–10 (1–10) visual analogue scale (VAS), using a random-effects model. MD > 0 means more pain after PCNL (favours RIRS).

Outcome: postoperative pain VAS on the day of surgery, extracted as the mean, SD and number of participants per arm.
- Day of surgery means the first postoperative pain assessment within about 24 hours of the procedure (e.g. 1 hour, 6 hours, 8 hours or 12 hours after surgery). If a study reports several times on the day of surgery, use the earliest one at or after 6 hours. If only a 1-hour value exists use that. Do not use a 24-hour, "first postoperative day morning" or 48-hour value; those belong to later days.
- If a study reports a single post-operative VAS without a time, treat it as the day-of-surgery value.
- Keep PCNL as the treatment arm and RIRS as the control arm. Check the table column headers and group definitions in each paper (some papers label RIRS as "Group 1"), and make the sign of the mean difference consistent: positive = higher pain with PCNL.
- Report all values on the same VAS direction (higher = more pain). Do not convert to other scales; if a study uses a 0–100 mm VAS, rescale to 0–10 and record the conversion.
- Extract SD, not SE; check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE.
- Trials with more than two arms: use only the PCNL-type and RIRS arms; ignore other techniques.

Do not pool pain on later days (day 1 or days 2–7), analgesic consumption, hospital stay, stone-free rate, complications, or operating time. Include only randomised trials in adults; exclude paediatric studies and comparisons with ESWL or open surgery.

title: Psychosocial interventions for survivors of rape and sexual assault experienced during adulthood
prompt:
What is the effect of psychosocial interventions (cognitive behavioural therapy including prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy and stress inoculation; behavioural and exposure-based therapies; eye-movement, memory-reconsolidation, neurofeedback or narrative exposure approaches; and brief or low-intensity interventions such as videos or computerised programmes), compared with an inactive control (wait-list, usual care, no treatment, or assessment only), on post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptom severity immediately after treatment in adults who have experienced rape or sexual assault?

Effect measure: pool as a standardised mean difference (SMD, Hedges' g) using a random-effects model. SMD < 0 means fewer PTSD symptoms with the psychosocial intervention (favours the intervention).

Outcome: PTSD symptom severity on a continuous scale, measured at the end of treatment (post-treatment), extracted as the mean, SD and number of participants per arm.
- If a trial reports several PTSD measures, use one per trial: prefer the clinician-administered scale (e.g. CAPS), otherwise the trial's primary self-report PTSD scale (e.g. PDS, PCL, PSS-SR, IES-R). Use total scores, not subscales.
- Use the first assessment after the intervention ended (post-treatment). Do not use follow-up assessments at 3, 6 or 12 months.
- Direction: all PTSD scales used here score more symptoms as higher; if a scale is scored the other way round, reverse its sign.
- If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n for that arm. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE. Use end-of-treatment values, not change scores, unless only change scores are reported.
- Multi-arm trials: include each eligible active arm as a separate comparison against the same inactive control, and divide the control group's size (and events) equally among those comparisons so control participants are not counted twice. Ignore arms that are active comparators (e.g. a different therapy given as the control).
- Use the number randomised or analysed as reported (intention-to-treat when available).
- Include only randomised controlled trials. Exclude reviews, non-randomised studies and trials whose control is an active treatment.

Do not pool depression, anxiety, dropout, quality of life, sleep or substance-use outcomes, or PTSD measured at follow-up. Include only adults (18 or over) who experienced sexual assault or rape in adulthood; exclude trials of childhood sexual abuse only, trials of military or combat trauma without sexual assault, and trials without an inactive control.

title: Musical and vocal interventions to improve neurodevelopmental outcomes for preterm infants
prompt: What is the effect of music or voice interventions (recorded music, live singing, parental voice or lullabies, with or without kangaroo care or skin-to-skin contact), compared with standard care or no music, on heart rate during the intervention in preterm infants (born before 37 weeks of gestation)?  Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in beats per minute (bpm) using the same pooling model the pipeline provides; report fixed-effect and random-effects estimates if both are available. MD < 0 means a lower heart rate with music (favours music).  Outcome: heart rate measured during the intervention session (while the music or voice is being delivered), extracted as the mean, SD and number of infants per arm. - Use heart rate recorded during the session. Do not use heart rate before the session, immediately after it, or at a later follow-up. - If a study reports both final values during the intervention and change from baseline, prefer the final value during the session. If only change from baseline is reported (mean change and SD of change), use those for both arms, and record that change scores were used. Do not mix a final value in one arm with a change score in the other. - If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE. - Heart rate must be in beats per minute; convert from other units if necessary. - Control: standard care, usual NICU environment, silence or no music. Exclude trials whose control is another active intervention. - If several music conditions are compared with one control (for example live and recorded music), combine them into one group or split the shared control equally among the comparisons so control infants are not counted twice. - Cross-over trials: if a paper reports results from the first period only, use that. If only combined paired data are reported, use the reported means and SDs and state that the data came from a cross-over design. - Use the number of infants randomised or analysed as reported, and assign arms by treatment description, not by column position. - Include only randomised controlled trials of preterm infants. Exclude trials in term infants or older children, studies without a standard-care or no-music control, and non-randomised studies.  Do not pool oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, pain scores, weight gain, length of stay, sleep, feeding or neurodevelopmental outcomes, or heart rate outside the intervention period.

title: Psychological interventions for depression and anxiety in patients with coronary heart disease, heart failure or atrial fibrillation
prompt: In adults with coronary heart disease, heart failure, or atrial fibrillation, what is the effect of a psychological intervention (delivered alone, with cardiac rehabilitation, or with pharmacotherapy) compared with no psychological intervention on depression symptoms at follow-up (6 to 12 months after randomisation)? Treat all validated depression measures (e.g., BDI, BDI-II, BDI-FS, CDS, HADS-D, HAM-D, PHQ-9, ZDS) as measures of one common depression construct and pool them using standardized mean difference (SMD) rather than separating by instrument. Use one eligible depression endpoint per intervention-control comparison, using the longest available eligible follow-up between 6 and 12 months. Evaluate ONLY depression. Do not extract, classify, or pool anxiety, health-related quality of life, self-efficacy, mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events, or any other outcome.

title: Skin care interventions in infants for preventing eczema and food allergy
prompt: What is the effect of skin care interventions (such as emollients) applied during infancy, compared with standard skin care or no skin care intervention, on the risk of developing eczema by 1 to 3 years of age in infants aged 12 months or younger?

title: Biosimilar monoclonal antibodies for cancer treatment in adults
prompt: What is the effect of bevacizumab biosimilar compared with bevacizumab originator on progression-free survival in adults with cancer? Extract the Hazard Ratio (HR) directly from each trial's own survival analysis (log[HR] + SE, or HR with 95% CI) — do not approximate it from other data.

title: Family-based interventions versus standard care for people with schizophrenia
prompt:
What is the effect of family-based interventions (psychoeducation, family support groups, family therapy or other structured programmes for relatives) delivered to the families of people with schizophrenia or related psychosis, compared with standard care, on caregiver burden in the family members measured up to one month after the end of the intervention?

Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in burden scale points, fixed-effect model if available, otherwise random effects. MD < 0 means lower caregiver burden with the family intervention (favours the intervention).

Outcome: family caregiver burden measured with a validated burden scale (for example the Family Burden Interview Schedule or a caregiver burden questionnaire), extracted as the mean, SD and number of family caregivers per arm.
- Use the first assessment after the intervention ended, within one month. Do not use later follow-up (1 to 6 months or longer), which belongs to separate analyses.
- Use the end-of-intervention value (mean and SD). If a trial reports only the change from baseline (mean change and SD of change), use those for both arms, and state that change scores were used. Do not mix an end value in one arm with a change score in the other.
- Use one burden measure per trial, preferring the total burden score. All scales are oriented so that a higher score means more burden; if a scale is oriented the other way, reverse its sign.
- If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE.
- Use the caregivers' scores (not the patients' symptom scores). If a trial reports separate results for several caregivers, use the main caregiver.
- Control: standard care or treatment as usual for the patient and family. Exclude trials whose control group receives another active family intervention.
- Multi-arm trials: include the family intervention arm and the standard-care arm only; combine several intervention arms into one group.
- Use the number randomised or analysed as reported; assign arms by treatment description, not by column position.
- Include only randomised controlled trials in families of people with schizophrenia or related psychosis. Exclude trials of patients' outcomes only and non-randomised studies.

Do not pool relapse, patient symptoms, patient functioning, family knowledge, expressed emotion, family coping or any other outcome.

title: Mobile health (m-health) smartphone interventions for adolescents and adults with overweight or obesity
prompt: In adults with overweight or obesity, what is the effect of a smartphone app intervention compared with no intervention or a minimal, non-app intervention (such as printed materials, a food diary, or usual care), on body weight in kilograms at short-term follow-up (3 to <6 months, preferably 3–4 months)? The comparator arm must be genuine no/minimal intervention — NOT another smartphone app or a different version of the same app; exclude any study where both arms receive a smartphone app. Use one endpoint per study; when a study reports both a follow-up value and a change-from-baseline value for the same outcome, prefer the change-from-baseline value. Do not extract, classify, or pool physical activity, BMI, self-efficacy, dietary behaviour, quality of life, or any other outcome, and exclude medium-term (6 months) or long-term (≥12 months) assessments.

title: Synbiotics, prebiotics and probiotics for people with chronic kidney disease
prompt:
What is the effect of probiotics (single-strain or multi-strain probiotic supplements, probiotic-containing foods such as probiotic yoghurt, soy milk or honey; not prebiotics or synbiotics) compared with placebo or no treatment on kidney function, measured as serum creatinine, at 8 to 24 weeks in people with chronic kidney disease (any stage, including diabetic nephropathy and dialysis)?

Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in mg/dL using a random-effects model. MD < 0 means lower serum creatinine with probiotics (favours probiotics).

Outcome: serum creatinine in mg/dL at the end of treatment, extracted as the mean, SD and number of participants per arm.
- Use the end-of-treatment value (mean and SD) when the paper reports one. If the paper reports only the change from baseline (mean change and SD of change) for each arm, use those instead, and record that change scores were used. Do not mix the end value of one arm with the change score of the other within a study.
- Treatment duration in the trial should be about 8 to 24 weeks; if a trial has more than one follow-up, use the last one within 24 weeks.
- Convert all values to mg/dL (µmol/L ÷ 88.4). Record the original unit and the conversion applied.
- If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n for that arm. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE.
- Read signs carefully: a change score is end minus baseline, so a fall in creatinine is negative. Do not drop minus signs, and do not read a decimal such as 0.2 as 2.
- Arms: assign probiotic vs placebo/no-treatment by group definition, not by column position. Many tables list the placebo group first. If the paper's table headings were lost in extraction, use the group definitions in the text to decide which column is which arm, and state that you inferred it.
- Trials with more than two arms: use the probiotic arm and the placebo/no-treatment arm; combine several probiotic arms by pooling means and SDs; ignore arms with other supplements.

Do not pool GFR/eGFR, albuminuria or proteinuria, inflammation markers, lipids, glucose, gut-microbiota outcomes or adverse events. Include only randomised controlled trials in people with CKD; exclude trials in people without kidney disease, trials of prebiotics or synbiotics, and comparisons between two probiotics.

title: Systemic corticosteroids for the prevention of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, a network meta-analysis
prompt: What is the effect of early (started before 7 days of postnatal age), low-dose systemic dexamethasone (cumulative dose below 2 mg/kg), compared with placebo or no treatment, on the combined outcome of death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age in preterm infants at risk of BPD?  Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) using a fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel model if available, otherwise random effects. RR < 1 means fewer infants died or had BPD with dexamethasone (favours dexamethasone).  Outcome: number of infants who died or had BPD at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age (events) out of the number randomised to each arm (total). - Use the combined outcome "death or BPD". Do not use BPD alone among survivors, death alone, or BPD at 28 days of age. - BPD at 36 weeks means oxygen requirement at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age; the number of infants dead before that time must be added to the number with BPD. If a paper reports death and BPD in survivors separately, sum them and use the number randomised as the denominator. - If a paper reports only "chronic lung disease at 36 weeks" or "oxygen dependence at 36 weeks" together with deaths, treat these as BPD. - Start of treatment must be before 7 days of life. Cumulative dexamethasone dose must be under 2 mg/kg over the whole course; compute the cumulative dose from the dose, schedule and duration given in the paper if it is not stated. Exclude trials whose cumulative dose is 2 mg/kg or more, or whose treatment begins at 7 days or later, from this group. - Control: placebo or no treatment. Exclude trials whose control is another steroid or a different dexamethasone dose. - Multi-arm trials: use the low-dose dexamethasone arm and the placebo/no-treatment arm only, and ignore other steroid arms (or combine arms that fall in the same dose category). - Assign arms by treatment description; use the number randomised as the denominator (intention-to-treat). - Include only randomised controlled trials in infants born before 37 weeks. Exclude trials of hydrocortisone, inhaled or intratracheal steroids, and trials of dexamethasone only for extubation in infants already ventilator-dependent after 7 days.  Do not pool BPD alone, mortality alone, cerebral palsy, neurodevelopmental outcome, infection, hypertension, hyperglycaemia or growth.

title: Erector spinae plane block for postoperative pain
prompt:
What is the effect of an ultrasound-guided erector spinae plane block (ESPB), compared with no block (general anaesthesia and usual analgesia only, without any injection), on cumulative postoperative opioid consumption at 24 hours in adults undergoing surgery?

Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in milligrams of oral morphine equivalents, using a random-effects model. MD < 0 means less opioid used with the ESPB (favours ESPB).

Outcome: cumulative postoperative opioid consumption over the first 24 hours after surgery (in the recovery room and on the ward, from patient-controlled analgesia and rescue doses), extracted as the mean, SD and number of participants per arm.
- Convert every opioid to oral morphine equivalents (mg) using standard published equianalgesic conversion ratios (for example for intravenous morphine, fentanyl, tramadol, pethidine, nalbuphine). Record the original drug, dose, unit and the conversion factor you used for each study. Do not mix raw units (mcg of fentanyl, mg of tramadol) in one pool.
- If a paper already reports morphine equivalents, use its values. If it reports consumption in more than one opioid, convert and sum them.
- If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE. If a paper reports median and interquartile range, estimate the mean and SD with a standard method and note it.
- Use the 24-hour value (cumulative from the end of surgery). Do not use 2-hour or 48-hour totals, and do not use intraoperative opioid doses.
- The control must be no block. Exclude trials whose control group received a sham or saline block, and trials comparing ESPB with another block or an epidural.
- Trials with several ESPB groups (different doses or approaches) against one control: combine the ESPB groups into one, or split the control group's size equally among the comparisons, so the control participants are not counted twice.
- Use the number randomised or analysed as reported; assign arms by treatment description, not by column position.
- Include only randomised controlled trials. Do not include review articles or meta-analyses, even if they cover the same procedure.

Do not pool pain scores, time to first analgesic request, nausea or vomiting, block-related complications, chronic pain or length of stay. Exclude studies in children and studies without a no-block control group.

title: Prophylactic use of inotropic agents for the prevention of low cardiac output syndrome and mortality in adults undergoing cardiac surgery
prompt:
What is the effect of levosimendan compared with placebo on all-cause mortality in adults
undergoing cardiac surgery? Pool as a Risk Ratio (RR) using each trial's reported deaths and
total randomized per arm. If a trial reports zero deaths in both arms, treat it as not
estimable and exclude it from pooling rather than continuity-corrected — expect this for at
least three of the trials in this review.

title: Addition of long-acting beta2 agonists or long-acting muscarinic antagonists versus doubling the dose of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) in adolescents and adults with uncontrolled asthma with medium dose ICS: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
prompt: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials in adolescents and adults with asthma that is uncontrolled on medium-dose inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), comparing a medium-dose ICS combined with a long-acting beta2 agonist (LABA) in one inhaler against the same medium-dose ICS alone (for example fluticasone propionate/salmeterol vs fluticasone propionate, budesonide/formoterol vs budesonide, fluticasone furoate/vilanterol vs fluticasone furoate, beclomethasone/formoterol vs beclomethasone, mometasone/indacaterol vs mometasone).  Outcome: moderate to severe asthma exacerbations, as the number of participants with at least one moderate or severe exacerbation during the trial, out of the number randomised in each arm.  Effect measure: Risk Ratio (RR), ICS/LABA versus ICS alone, using participant counts. Values below 1 favour ICS/LABA.  Outcome rules: - Treatment arm = medium-dose ICS plus LABA. Control arm = the same medium-dose ICS alone, at the same dose. Ignore arms that are high-dose ICS, ICS plus LAMA, or any other comparator. - If a trial has several arms (for example a high-dose ICS arm or a high-dose ICS/LABA arm), use only the medium-dose ICS/LABA arm and the medium-dose ICS arm. If a control arm is shared with other comparisons, use its full reported size and events. - Count participants with at least one moderate or severe exacerbation (events needing systemic corticosteroids, an emergency visit or a hospital stay). If a trial reports only severe exacerbations or reports several definitions, use the definition closest to "moderate or severe". If it reports exacerbation rates only (events per person-year), use the participant counts if given in the text. - Use the full treatment period. - Use the number randomised or analysed as reported (intention-to-treat when available).  Include all randomised trials in the uploaded papers that fit this description. Do not exclude a trial because of its LABA or ICS brand, its dose schedule, its duration, or its size. Exclude only reviews, protocols and trials with no medium-dose ICS-alone control.

title: Shared decision-making for supporting women’s decisions about breast cancer screening
prompt:
What is the effect of decision aids or other interventions that only enhance communication about breast cancer screening (information on benefits and harms given without an explicit exercise to clarify the woman's values and preferences), compared with usual information or control, on women's knowledge about breast cancer screening (mammography) measured as a continuous score?

Effect measure: pool as a standardised mean difference (SMD, Hedges' g) using a random-effects model, because the knowledge questionnaires use different scales. SMD > 0 means better knowledge with the intervention (favours the intervention).

Outcome: a continuous knowledge score about screening (for example the number of correct answers on a questionnaire about benefits, harms, overdiagnosis and screening interval), extracted as the post-intervention mean, SD and number of women per arm.
- Use one overall knowledge score per trial (for example conceptual plus numerical knowledge, or total knowledge items), preferring the total score over sub-scales. All scales are oriented so that a higher score means more knowledge; if a scale is oriented the other way, reverse its sign.
- Use the first assessment after the intervention, from immediately after up to about one month. Do not use later follow-up.
- If a paper gives a mean difference with a confidence interval or p-value but no SD, derive the SD: for two groups, SD ≈ √n × (CI width) ÷ 3.92 for each group (or from the p-value and sample sizes), and state that the SD was derived.
- If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE.
- For cluster-randomised trials, adjust the sample size by the design effect (1 + (average cluster size − 1) × ICC) using the ICC reported, or state an assumed value.
- Use the number analysed per arm; if only the number randomised is given for this outcome, use it and say so.
- Include only trials of interventions that focus on improving communication or information (decision aids, leaflets or consultations with benefit and harm information) without a values-clarification component. Exclude trials whose intervention includes an explicit exercise to clarify values and preferences, which are a separate comparison.
- Control: usual information, standard leaflet, or no intervention.
- Multi-arm trials: include the communication-only arm and the control arm; combine several communication arms into one group.
- Include only randomised controlled trials in women eligible for breast cancer screening.

Do not pool informed choice, decisional conflict, anxiety, intention to be screened, screening uptake or any other outcome.

title: Prevention of self-harm and suicide in young people up to the age of 25 in education settings
prompt: What is the effect of indicated interventions (interventions targeting young people up to age 25 who are already showing early signs or symptoms of risk, such as existing suicidal ideation or self-harm history — as distinct from universal interventions delivered to everyone regardless of risk, or selective interventions targeting at-risk groups who are not yet symptomatic), compared with control, on suicidal ideation measured immediately at the end of the intervention (postintervention), in education settings?  This is specifically the POSTINTERVENTION timepoint — do not include short-term (1-3 months), medium-term (4-12 months), or longest-follow-up suicidal ideation measurements; those are separate outcomes in this review.  Note on scale direction: a LOWER suicidal ideation score means a BETTER outcome — code the effect size so a positive value means the indicated intervention reduced suicidal ideation more than control.  Note on multi-arm trials: if a trial has more than one indicated-intervention arm compared against a single shared control group (e.g. two different intervention types tested against one common control), extract each intervention arm as its own separate row against that same shared control — do not merge the two intervention arms together, and do not pick only one and discard the other.  If a study does not report the number of participants in each group separately (only a total), and the trial was randomized, you may assume an even 50/50 split between groups unless the paper states otherwise — note this assumption explicitly when you make it.

title: Psychological therapies delivered remotely for the management of chronic pain (excluding headache) in adults
prompt: What is the effect of remotely delivered cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT; internet-based, telephone-based, app-based or video-delivered, including acceptance and commitment or exposure-based variants with a cognitive-behavioural basis), compared with treatment as usual or a waiting-list control, on functional disability at the end of treatment in adults with chronic non-headache pain (for example low back pain, fibromyalgia, osteoarthritis or mixed chronic pain)?  Effect measure: pool as a standardised mean difference (SMD, Hedges' g) using a random-effects model. SMD < 0 means less disability with CBT (favours CBT).  Outcome: functional disability or physical functioning, extracted as the post-treatment mean, SD and number of participants per arm. - Use one disability or physical-function measure per trial, preferring a disability-specific scale (for example the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire, Pain Disability Index, Oswestry, WHO-DAS or similar) over a general quality-of-life subscale; if only a general physical-function subscale is reported (for example SF-36 or SF-12 physical function), use that. - Direction: on disability scales a higher score means more disability. On physical-function scales (for example SF-36, SF-12 physical function) a higher score means better function. Reverse the sign of the means of scales where higher is better (multiply by −1) so that a lower value always means less disability, before computing the SMD. - Use the first assessment after the treatment ended (post-treatment; typically 3 to 24 weeks after randomisation). Do not use longer follow-up assessments. - If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE. - Control: treatment as usual, waiting list, or usual care plus waiting list. Exclude trials whose control is an active therapy (for example another psychological treatment or an attention control). - Multi-arm trials: if there are several remote CBT arms (for example with different levels of therapist contact), combine them into one CBT group (pool means and SDs, sum participants) and compare with the shared control once. - Use the number randomised or analysed as reported; assign arms by treatment description, not by column position. - Include only randomised controlled trials of remotely delivered CBT in adults. Exclude face-to-face therapy, trials in children, and headache or migraine trials.  Do not pool pain intensity, pain improvement, quality of life, mood, anxiety, adverse events or any outcome other than functional disability.

title: Telerehabilitation for neck pain
prompt: In adults with chronic neck pain, what is the effect of telerehabilitation delivering exercise or physical activity, compared with a minimal intervention (advice, educational materials, usual care without active rehabilitation, wait-list, or no active care), on pain intensity at short-term follow-up (more than 2 weeks and no later than 3 months after randomisation)? If a study has more than two arms, extract ONLY the isolated pairwise comparison between the telerehabilitation-exercise arm and the genuine minimal/no-intervention control arm — never a comparison between two active intervention arms, and never an omnibus statistic (e.g., a Kruskal-Wallis or ANOVA test spanning all groups). If the paper's own reported numbers (e.g., medians) appear to contradict its own stated direction of effect, do not extract that result — treat it as unusable rather than force a computation. Use one endpoint per study. Do not extract, classify, or pool function, quality of life, anxiety, depression, fear avoidance, adherence, or any other outcome.

title: Standard- versus extended-duration anticoagulation for primary venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in acutely ill medical patients
prompt: What is the effect of extended-duration anticoagulation, compared with standard-duration anticoagulation, on major bleeding within 45 days (short-term) in acutely ill medical patients receiving venous thromboembolism prophylaxis? This is the single target outcome: major bleeding, short-term (45 days or fewer), from the PRIMARY analysis only. Do NOT include the COVID-19-only sensitivity analysis, the same-extended-agent sensitivity analysis, or any subgroup analysis (by sex, age, cancer history, D-dimer status, or infection status) — these are separate, related analyses in this review using the same outcome label. Do NOT include symptomatic VTE, all-cause mortality, or any long-term (more than 45 days) outcome. This is dichotomous (event/no-event) data — please pool it as a Risk Ratio (RR), using each trial's reported number of major bleeding events and total randomized per arm. Note: extended-duration anticoagulation is the treatment/intervention arm, but for this particular outcome a HIGHER event rate is the worse (harmful) result for it — major bleeding is a safety/harm outcome, not a benefit outcome, so do not assume the treatment arm having more events is an extraction error. Note: if a trial reports zero major bleeding events in BOTH arms, that is expected for at least two of the trials in this review and should be treated as "not estimable" for this ratio measure, excluded from pooling rather than continuity-corrected.

title: Exercise training for adults undergoing maintenance dialysis
prompt: What is the effect of exercise training (aerobic, resistance, combined or other structured exercise, delivered during or between dialysis sessions), compared with no exercise or a placebo exercise (such as stretching or sham exercise), on lower-limb functional strength measured by the sit-to-stand test in adults receiving maintenance dialysis (haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis)?  Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in seconds using a random-effects model. MD < 0 means a shorter time (better performance) with exercise (favours exercise). Report the difference as exercise minus control.  Outcome: the time in seconds to complete five repetitions of the sit-to-stand test, extracted as the mean, SD and number of participants per arm. - Use the five-repetition (or five to ten repetition) timed sit-to-stand test, where the result is a time in seconds. Do not use the 30-second or 60-second test, where the result is a count of repetitions in a fixed time, and do not use the timed up-and-go or six-minute walk test. - Use the end-of-intervention value (mean and SD). If a trial reports only the change from baseline (mean change and SD of change), use those for both arms and state it. Do not mix an end value in one arm with a change score in the other. - If a trial reports several time points during the intervention, use the one at the end of the exercise programme. Do not use follow-up after the programme ended. - If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE. - Convert times to seconds. If a paper reports the result as a number of repetitions per time, leave it out of this outcome. - Control: usual care or no exercise, or a placebo exercise. Exclude trials whose control group does a different active exercise or receives another active intervention. - Multi-arm and factorial trials: combine several exercise arms into one exercise group (pool means and SDs, sum participants), and combine several control arms into one control group, or take the arm that matches the question and state the choice. For trials with several exercise arms and one control group, use the control group once. - Use the number randomised or analysed as reported; assign arms by treatment description, not by column position. - Include only randomised controlled trials in adults on maintenance dialysis. Exclude kidney transplant recipients, people with non-dialysis kidney disease, and non-randomised studies. Theses and dissertations that report a randomised trial are eligible.  Do not pool the 30-second sit-to-stand count, blood pressure, quality of life, dialysis adequacy, adverse events or any non-sit-to-stand outcome.

title: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) with and without exercise to reduce fear of falling in older people living in the community
prompt: What is the effect of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) interventions, delivered alone or combined with exercise (e.g. a cognitive-behavioural or multicomponent programme such as "A Matter of Balance", behaviour-change/motivational support, Tai Chi plus CBT), compared with control (usual care, no intervention, or an attention/discussion/education control), on fear of falling in community-dwelling older people, measured immediately after the intervention?  Effect measure: pool as a standardised mean difference (SMD, Hedges' g) using a random-effects model. SMD < 0 means less fear of falling in the intervention arm (favours intervention).  Outcome: fear of falling / falls-related self-efficacy, extracted as the post-intervention mean, SD and number of participants per arm. - Scale direction: on FES-I and similar concern scales a higher score means more fear; on confidence scales (e.g. FES-S, mFES, ABC) a higher score means more confidence/less fear. Reverse the sign of confidence scales (multiply by −1) so that a lower value always means less fear before computing the SMD. - If a study reports several fear-of-falling measures, use one per study in this order of preference: FES-I (and its short form), then modified FES / FES / Swedish FES-S / ABC, then a single-item fear question. - Use the first assessment after the intervention ended, within about one month of its end where possible. If a study only reports later follow-ups, use the earliest one. Do not use the 6-month or longer follow-up when an earlier post-intervention value exists. - Use post-intervention scores rather than change scores when both are reported. - Multi-arm trials: include every arm that has a CBT or behaviour-change component (CBT only, CBT with exercise, CBT with Tai Chi, exercise with motivational interviewing). Exclude exercise-only arms with no behavioural component. If two eligible arms share one control group, divide the control group's sample size equally between the comparisons so the control participants are not counted twice. - Cluster-randomised trials: use the cluster-adjusted results when the paper reports them; if the paper ignores clustering, reduce the sample sizes accordingly and state the adjustment. - Multiple reports of the same trial: extract once. Use the short-term or primary report for the post-intervention timepoint.  Do not pool follow-up timepoints beyond the first post-intervention assessment, activity avoidance, depression, anxiety, quality of life, falls count, or adverse events. Include only randomised trials in people aged 60 or over living in the community. Exclude exercise-only, education-only, home-modification or hip-protector interventions with no CBT component.

title: Interleukin-receptor antagonist and tumour necrosis factor inhibitors for the primary and secondary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases
prompt: What is the effect of interleukin-1 receptor antagonists, compared with placebo or usual care, on all-cause mortality, for secondary prevention in people with established cardiovascular disease? Include both anakinra and canakinumab as sub-types of this drug class, keeping them as separate subgroups within the same pooled analysis.

title: Statins for the primary prevention of venous thromboembolism
prompt: What is the effect of statins compared with placebo on deep vein thrombosis (DVT), stratified by type of statin (rosuvastatin, atorvastatin, pravastatin), for the primary prevention of venous thromboembolism? Pool as an Odds Ratio (OR) using each trial's reported DVT events and total randomized per arm, keeping the three statin types as separate subgroups rather than combining them into one pooled estimate, since they show materially different (and in one case opposite-direction) effects.

title: Platinum-based chemotherapy for early triple-negative breast cancer
prompt:
What is the effect of adding platinum-based chemotherapy (carboplatin or cisplatin) to neoadjuvant (pre-operative) chemotherapy, compared with the same neoadjuvant chemotherapy without platinum, on disease-free survival in women with early-stage triple-negative breast cancer?

Effect measure: pool as a hazard ratio (HR) using a fixed-effect inverse-variance model on the log hazard ratio (or random effects if fixed-effect is not available). HR < 1 means longer disease-free survival with platinum (favours platinum).

Outcome: disease-free survival (also reported as event-free survival, relapse-free survival or invasive disease-free survival) as a hazard ratio with its 95% confidence interval, comparing the platinum arm with the control arm.
- Use the hazard ratio and 95% confidence interval reported in the paper (convert the confidence interval to a standard error of the log HR). Do not rebuild a hazard ratio from event counts. If a paper reports only Kaplan-Meier curves and numbers at risk, leave the study out.
- Platinum arm = the group that received carboplatin or cisplatin; control arm = the group that received the same regimen without platinum. Orient the HR as platinum versus control, and invert it (HR to 1/HR, with the interval swapped) if the paper reports control versus platinum.
- Use the longest follow-up reported in the trial for disease-free survival. If a paper reports both a pathological complete response analysis and a later long-term analysis, use the long-term survival HR.
- Trials with two platinum arms that share one control group (for example carboplatin alone and carboplatin plus another agent, each versus the same control): include each comparison separately against the control, and note that the control group is shared.
- If a trial reports event-free survival that includes events such as progression before surgery and also a disease-free survival, prefer disease-free survival.
- Include only randomised controlled trials in which neoadjuvant treatment is given before surgery. Exclude trials where platinum is given only after surgery (adjuvant), trials mixing neoadjuvant and adjuvant treatment, and trials without a platinum-free control arm.

Do not pool pathological complete response, overall survival, toxicity or any outcome other than disease-free survival. Include only women with triple-negative breast cancer; exclude trials restricted to HER2-positive disease or to other cancers.

title: Continuous infusion versus bolus injection of loop diuretics for acute heart failure
prompt: What is the effect of continuous intravenous infusion of a loop diuretic (furosemide, torsemide or bumetanide), compared with intermittent bolus injection of the same loop diuretic, on net weight loss in kilograms in adults hospitalised with acute heart failure?  Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in kilograms using a random-effects model. Orient the difference as continuous infusion minus bolus, so MD > 0 means more weight lost with continuous infusion (favours continuous infusion).  Outcome: net weight loss in kilograms during the treatment period, extracted as the mean, SD and number of participants per arm. Weight loss is a positive number (kilograms lost). - Use the weight loss over the period each trial reports (for example at 72 hours, until discharge, or until decompensation or resolution of congestion). If a trial reports several periods, use the longest period that is still within the hospital stay, and state the period used. - If weight is reported as a change, make sure it is positive for weight lost; reverse the sign if the paper reports weight change as negative for loss. Do not use change in weight as a percentage. - Convert pounds to kilograms (÷ 2.205). - If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. If a median with interquartile range is reported, estimate the mean and SD with a standard method and say so. - If the number analysed per arm is not stated for weight loss, use the number randomised to each arm and say so. - Factorial and multi-arm trials (for example continuous versus bolus crossed with low versus high dose): combine the dose arms within each delivery mode, so that all continuous-infusion participants are one group and all bolus participants are the other; sum participants, and pool means and SDs. - Compare only continuous infusion with bolus of the same loop diuretic; exclude trials that compare a loop diuretic with another drug, with ultrafiltration, or with placebo. - Assign arms by delivery mode, not by column position. - Include only randomised controlled trials in hospitalised adults with acute heart failure.  Do not pool urine output, fluid balance, mortality, length of stay, readmission, renal function or any other outcome.

title: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents for preventing acute kidney injury
prompt:
What is the effect of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (epoetin alfa, beta or zeta, darbepoetin, methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta or other ESAs), compared with placebo or usual care without an ESA, on the incidence of acute kidney injury (AKI) in people at risk of AKI (for example after cardiac surgery, in critical illness or trauma, after contrast exposure, or after kidney transplantation)?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) of AKI, ESA divided by control, using a random-effects model. RR < 1 means fewer participants with AKI with an ESA (favours ESA).

Outcome: the number of participants who developed acute kidney injury (events) out of the number randomised to each arm (total), during the trial's follow-up.
- Use the trial's own definition of AKI (for example KDIGO, AKIN or RIFLE criteria, or a rise in serum creatinine above a stated threshold, or a fall in estimated GFR), and state which definition was used. If a trial reports AKI under more than one definition, prefer the standard consensus criteria (KDIGO, then AKIN, then RIFLE), and otherwise the primary definition.
- Count participants with AKI, not episodes. Do not use need for dialysis, serum creatinine as a continuous value, or "kidney dysfunction" without a defined threshold as AKI.
- If a trial reports no AKI in either arm, record zero events with the arm sizes and keep the trial visible. If AKI is not reported, leave the trial out and say so.
- Use the number randomised as the denominator (intention-to-treat). If the paper reports only the number analysed, use that and state it.
- Control: placebo or usual care (no ESA). Exclude trials whose control group receives another active kidney-protective drug.
- Multi-arm trials: include the ESA arm and the control arm only; combine several ESA doses into one group (sum events and participants).
- Assign arms by treatment, not by column position.
- Include only randomised controlled trials in adults or children, in any setting, where the ESA was given to prevent AKI or to treat another condition and AKI was recorded.

Do not pool mortality, dialysis requirement, haemoglobin, transfusion, thromboembolic events or length of stay.

title: Vocabulary interventions for second language (L2) learners up to six years of age
cochrane_topic: Mental health, behavioural and neurodevelopmental conditions
prompt:
What is the effect of vocabulary interventions (for example shared book reading, dialogic reading, explicit word teaching or dual-language instruction) delivered to children up to six years of age who are learning a second language (L2), compared with standard care or no intervention, on their expressive vocabulary in the second language for words that were not directly taught (distal vocabulary), measured immediately after the intervention?

Effect measure: pool as a standardised mean difference (SMD, Hedges' g) using a random-effects model. SMD > 0 means better expressive second-language vocabulary in the intervention group (favours the intervention).

Outcome: expressive vocabulary in the second language on a measure of general or untaught words, extracted as the post-intervention mean, SD and number of children per arm.
- Distal vocabulary means a standardised or general vocabulary test that was not tailored to the words taught in the intervention (for example a standardised naming or picture vocabulary test), as opposed to proximal vocabulary, which is a test of the words taught. Do not use tests built from the taught words.
- Expressive means the child has to produce the word (naming, labelling or defining), as opposed to receptive tests where the child points to or recognises the word. Do not use receptive measures.
- The language is the second language being learned (the societal or school language), not the first language. Do not use first-language outcomes.
- Use the first assessment after the intervention ended (post-test). Do not use delayed follow-up assessments.
- If a trial reports several distal expressive measures, use one per trial: the standardised, broadest one. If a trial reports only a total score across receptive and expressive tasks, leave it out.
- If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Use post-test values; if only adjusted means from a model are reported, use those and note it.
- Cluster-randomised trials: use cluster-adjusted results if the paper reports them. Otherwise adjust the sample sizes by the design effect, 1 + (average cluster size − 1) × ICC, using the ICC reported or an assumed ICC of 0.15, and state which was used.
- Control: standard care, usual classroom instruction or no intervention. Exclude trials whose control group receives another vocabulary intervention.
- Multi-arm trials: combine intervention arms into one group (pool means and SDs, sum participants), or pick the arm that matches the review question and state the choice; use the control group once.
- Include only randomised controlled trials in children up to six years old learning a second language. Exclude trials in monolingual children and trials in older children.

Do not pool receptive vocabulary, taught-word (proximal) vocabulary, first-language outcomes, follow-up assessments, or non-vocabulary outcomes such as reading or phonological awareness.

title: Zinc for prevention and treatment of the common cold
prompt:
What is the effect of zinc (oral lozenges, tablets or intranasal preparations), compared with placebo, on the duration of the common cold in people with a naturally acquired cold (treatment trials)?

Measurement: mean duration of the cold in days, from the start of treatment (or symptom onset, as defined by each trial) to resolution of the cold, as the mean difference between groups. Do not pool the proportion with ongoing symptoms at the end of the study, severity scores, duration of individual symptoms, adverse events, prevention trials or any other outcome.

title: Educational and psychological interventions for managing atopic dermatitis (eczema)
prompt:
What is the effect of group educational interventions, compared with standard care only, on
quality of life (DLQI - Dermatology Life Quality Index or its infant/family variants) in
people with a dermatological condition?

One trial (Liang 2017) reports separate DLQI results for two different age-stratified
sub-populations (children and infants) — extract both as separate rows rather than picking
only one or averaging them together, since this review pools them as distinct comparisons
within the same outcome.

Do not include other quality-of-life outcome definitions or scales from this review (e.g. a
different DLQI subscale or a different respondent) — this is specifically the "all scales,
infants, children, and family" version of the outcome.

title: Anti-seizure medications for neonates with seizures
prompt:
What is the effect of phenobarbital compared with levetiracetam, each used as first-line anti-seizure medication, on all-cause mortality before hospital discharge in neonates (up to 28 days of age, term or preterm) with clinically or electrographically diagnosed seizures?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR), phenobarbital divided by levetiracetam. RR > 1 means more deaths with phenobarbital (favours levetiracetam).

Outcome: number of infants who died from any cause between randomisation and hospital discharge (events) out of the number randomised or analysed in each arm (total).
- Use deaths during the initial hospital stay or NICU stay. Do not use mortality at 3, 6 or 12 months, or deaths after discharge.
- If a paper reports a count of zero deaths in an arm, record it as zero events with the arm's size (do not drop the study). If a paper does not report deaths at all, leave the study out rather than assuming zero.
- Be careful with arm labels. Many papers list levetiracetam first in tables or figures; assign arms by drug name from the group definitions, not by column position, and keep phenobarbital (or phenobarbitone) as the treatment group in every study.
- Use the number randomised to each arm as the denominator when the paper gives it; otherwise the number analysed.
- Trials in which infants who did not respond were switched to the other drug (cross-over or add-on): use the original randomised group for each infant.
- Multi-arm trials: include only the phenobarbital and levetiracetam arms. Ignore arms with other drugs (e.g. midazolam, phenytoin, topiramate, lidocaine).

Do not pool seizure control, time to seizure cessation, EEG outcomes, adverse events, neurodevelopmental outcomes or mechanical ventilation. Include only randomised or quasi-randomised trials in neonates; exclude trials of seizure prophylaxis, trials in which neither arm is phenobarbital or levetiracetam, and comparisons of the two drugs as add-on therapy after failure of a first drug.

title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for post-traumatic stress disorder in adults
prompt: What is the effect of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS, including deep TMS and theta-burst stimulation), compared with sham stimulation, on PTSD symptom severity in adults with post-traumatic stress disorder, measured as the change from baseline to the assessment immediately after treatment?  Effect measure: pool as a standardised mean difference (SMD, Hedges' g) using a random-effects model. SMD < 0 means a greater reduction in PTSD symptoms with active rTMS (favours rTMS).  Outcome: change in PTSD symptom severity from baseline to immediately after the course of treatment, on the trial's primary validated PTSD scale (for example the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale, the PTSD Checklist, or the Davidson Trauma Scale), extracted as the mean change, SD of change and number of participants per arm. - Use the intention-to-treat (all randomised, or all analysed in the trial's primary analysis) result. Accept the trial's own primary analysis (for example a mixed model, last observation carried forward, multiple imputation or "all randomised participants analysed") even if the method for missing data is not named in detail. Do not require an explicit statement of imputation. - If the paper reports baseline and post-treatment means and SDs per arm but not the change, calculate the mean change as post-treatment minus baseline for each arm. Estimate the SD of the change from the baseline and post-treatment SDs, assuming a correlation of 0.5 between the two measurements, and state that the change and its SD were derived. - If the paper reports the mean change and SD of change directly, use them. - If variability is reported as SE or SEM, convert to SD = SE × √n. Check table footnotes for whether "±" is SD or SE. - Use the assessment closest to the end of the treatment course (immediately after treatment). Do not use follow-up assessments weeks or months later. - Use the scale on which a higher score means worse PTSD; if a scale is oriented the other way, reverse its sign. - Use the number randomised or analysed in the primary analysis for each arm. If arm sizes are not stated in the text, use the sizes in the participant-flow diagram or the table of results. - Control: sham rTMS (a sham coil or sham stimulation). Exclude trials with no sham arm. - Multi-arm trials: include the active rTMS arm and the sham arm only; if there are two active arms, combine them into one group (sum participants) and use the sham group once. - Include only randomised sham-controlled trials in adults with PTSD. Exclude open-label and uncontrolled studies.  Do not pool depression, anxiety, quality of life, adverse events, dropouts, or any non-PTSD outcome.

title: Diclofenac for acute postoperative pain in children
prompt: What is the effect of diclofenac (any route: rectal, intravenous, intramuscular, oral; given before, during or after surgery) compared with an opioid analgesic (e.g. morphine, fentanyl, sufentanil, pethidine/meperidine, papaveretum, nalbuphine; any route including caudal/epidural) on the number of children who required rescue analgesic medication after surgery, in children aged under 18 undergoing any surgical procedure under general anaesthesia?  Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) using a random-effects model. RR < 1 means fewer children needing rescue analgesia in the diclofenac arm (favours diclofenac).  Outcome: number of children (events) and number randomised/analysed (total) in each arm who received any rescue or supplementary analgesic after surgery (also described as "analgesic complementation", "supplementary analgesia", "postoperative analgesia given", or "number requiring [opioid/paracetamol] postoperatively"), within the first 24 hours after surgery. - Use the count covering the longest postoperative window available up to 24 hours (e.g. recovery ward stay, first 4 hours, until discharge, 24 hours). Do not use a count limited to the first 2 hours when a longer window is also reported. - If the numbers are only given as percentages, convert them to counts using the group size. If they appear only in a figure or bar chart, read the percentage for each group from the figure and convert it to counts; do not exclude the study for that reason. - Multi-arm trials: use the diclofenac arm as the treatment group. Combine all opioid arms into one control group (sum events and totals). Ignore no-analgesia/placebo arms, local anaesthetic arms (e.g. caudal bupivacaine alone), paracetamol arms and other NSAID arms. - Extract from each study the single dichotomous rescue-analgesia count. Do not substitute time to first rescue analgesia, rescue dose consumed, or pain scores.  Do not pool pain intensity scores, time to rescue medication, opioid consumption, nausea/vomiting, bleeding or other adverse events. Exclude comparisons of diclofenac against placebo, paracetamol, other NSAIDs or local anaesthetics, and exclude studies in adults.

title: Prophylactic anticoagulants for non-hospitalised people with COVID-19
prompt: What is the effect of prophylactic anticoagulants (low-molecular-weight heparin, rivaroxaban, apixaban, aspirin or similar given to prevent thrombosis), compared with placebo or no treatment, on adverse events in non-hospitalised adults with COVID-19, including outpatients and people after hospital discharge?  Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) using a random-effects model. RR > 1 means more adverse events with the anticoagulant.  Outcome: the number of participants who had at least one adverse event (events) out of the number randomised to each arm (total), during the follow-up period. - Use the trial's overall count of participants with adverse events of any type. If a trial reports only serious adverse events, or only bleeding events (major, clinically relevant non-major or any bleeding), use that count as the trial's adverse event outcome, and state which definition was used. If a trial reports several categories, prefer the broadest ("any adverse event"), and otherwise sum only categories that the paper defines as non-overlapping. - Count participants, not events. If a paper gives only the number of events (episodes), leave the trial out. - Do not use death, hospitalisation, venous thromboembolism or other efficacy outcomes as adverse events. - Use the number randomised as the denominator (intention-to-treat). If the paper's safety population is smaller, use the safety population only when the number randomised is not given, and say so. - Control: placebo or no anticoagulant (standard care). Exclude trials whose control is another anticoagulant or a different dose of the same anticoagulant. - Multi-arm trials: include the anticoagulant arm and the placebo/no-treatment arm; combine several anticoagulant doses into one group (sum events and participants). - Treat several PDFs of the same trial (a journal article and a publisher or repository copy of it) as one study. - Include only randomised controlled trials of non-hospitalised adults, including people after discharge. Exclude trials of hospitalised patients, and non-randomised studies.  Do not pool mortality, thrombosis, hospitalisation, symptom resolution or quality of life.

title: Sympathetic nerve blocks for persistent pain in adults with inoperable abdominopelvic cancer
prompt: What is the effect of a single sympathetic nerve block, compared with standard care, on pain score at 14 days? Do not include pain score at other timepoints (e.g. 1 month) — those are separate analyses in this review.

title: Autoinflation for otitis media with effusion (OME) in children
prompt:
What is the effect of autoinflation (children inflating the middle ear through the nose using a balloon, a carnival blower or a commercial device), compared with watchful waiting or no treatment, on the persistence of otitis media with effusion (OME) in children at up to 6 weeks of follow-up?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) using a random-effects model. RR < 1 means less persistent effusion with autoinflation (favours autoinflation).

Outcome: number of children (or ears, as reported) with persistent middle ear effusion at the first follow-up at or before 6 weeks (events) out of the number in each arm (total).
- Persistence is a flat tympanogram (type B), type B or C2, or effusion still seen on pneumatic otoscopy. Resolution or improvement is the opposite. If a paper reports how many resolved or improved, convert it to persistence as total minus resolved. If it reports persistence directly, use that.
- Use the follow-up closest to 4 weeks within the window of 2 to 6 weeks; if a paper reports several times in that window, use the latest one.
- Unit of analysis: if a paper reports data per ear for children with bilateral disease, adjust for the correlation between the two ears of the same child. Divide both events and total by the design effect, 1 + (average ears per child − 1) × 0.5, and say that the adjustment was applied. If the paper reports persistence per child, use that directly without adjustment.
- If a paper reports both per-ear and per-child data, prefer per-child.
- Control: watchful waiting, no treatment or standard care only. Exclude trials whose control is sham autoinflation, another active treatment or placebo.
- Treat different reports of the same trial (for example a journal paper and a funder's monograph) as one study for the main trial, but a separate pilot trial that is described in the same report counts as its own study.
- Multi-arm trials: include only the autoinflation arm and the no-treatment arm.

Do not pool hearing outcomes, symptom or quality-of-life scores, adverse events, or persistence at 6 weeks to 3 months or later. Include only randomised controlled trials in children (under 18) with OME; exclude trials of adults, of surgical treatments, and of autoinflation as an add-on to other treatment in only one arm.

title: Topical and oral steroids for otitis media with effusion (OME) in children
prompt: What is the effect of intranasal steroids (e.g. mometasone, beclomethasone, budesonide, fluticasone), with or without other treatments given equally to both arms, compared with no steroid treatment (no treatment, or the same co-treatment alone), on persistence of otitis media with effusion (OME) in children at up to 1 month?  Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) using a random-effects model. RR < 1 means fewer children/ears with persistent effusion in the steroid arm (favours steroids).  Outcome: number with persistent middle ear effusion at the first assessment up to 1 month (≤ 6 weeks) after starting treatment, extracted as event counts per arm (events and total for steroid and control). - Persistence = effusion still present at follow-up: tympanogram type B (or type C2 / non-type-A if that is how the study defines failure), "not cured", "no improvement", or "persistent effusion". Resolution/cure = type A tympanogram or complete clearance. If a study reports resolution or improvement, convert it to persistence as total minus resolved. - If the headline result is a multi-category or ordinal scale (e.g. complete remission / partial remission / no change / exacerbation), do not discard the study. Look for a table of post-treatment tympanogram types or cure/no-cure counts per arm and derive persistence counts from it. - Unit of analysis: use children if reported per child. If results are reported per ear, use ears and combine right and left ears (sum both ears' events and totals). Never use one ear only. - If a trial has more than two arms, use only the intranasal-steroid arm and the no-steroid arm that received the same co-treatment. Ignore oral-steroid, montelukast, antihistamine-only or other active arms.  Do not pool hearing thresholds/air-bone gap, symptom or parent-reported improvement, quality of life, adverse events, or results after 6 weeks. Exclude oral or systemic steroid trials and trials whose control arm is a placebo spray.

title: Lay health workers in primary and community health care for maternal and child health: identification and treatment of wasting in children
prompt:
What is the effect of treatment of wasting (acute malnutrition, including severe and moderate acute malnutrition) in children aged 6 to 59 months delivered by lay health workers (community health workers, volunteers or other non-professional providers), compared with treatment delivered by health professionals in health facilities, on recovery from wasting?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) of recovery, lay health worker arm divided by health professional arm, using a random-effects model on the log risk ratio. RR > 1 means higher recovery with lay health workers.

Outcome: the proportion of children who recovered or were cured at the end of treatment (events out of the number of children treated in each arm). Use the trial's own definition of recovery or cure (for example reaching a weight-for-height or mid-upper-arm-circumference threshold, or being discharged as cured). If a trial reports several recovery measures, use the cure rate for the whole programme (not a subgroup), and if only a risk ratio is reported, use it.
- Compute the RR from the numbers cured and the number of children treated in each arm (intention-to-treat where available). Orient it as lay health workers versus health professionals, and invert it if a paper reports the reverse.
- Do not use defaulting, death, relapse, weight gain, length of stay or coverage as the outcome.
- Cluster designs: when children are treated within clusters (health facilities, communities or districts), adjust the standard error of the log RR for clustering. Multiply its variance by the design effect, 1 + (average cluster size − 1) × ICC, using the ICC reported by the trial; if none is reported, state that an assumed ICC of 0.02 was used and report a sensitivity analysis with 0.05.
- If a trial already reports a cluster-adjusted RR with confidence interval, use that and do not adjust again.
- Include trials with a lay-health-worker-delivered treatment arm and a health-professional-delivered control arm: randomised trials, cluster-randomised trials, and controlled before-after or non-randomised comparative studies. Assign arms by who delivered the treatment, not by column position.
- Multi-arm trials: include only the lay health worker arm and the health professional arm.

Do not pool outcomes other than recovery from wasting (for example improvement from severe wasting in a single trial, coverage, defaulting, mortality or relapse). Exclude trials in which both arms are delivered by lay workers, trials in adults, and trials of prevention only.

title: Interventions to prevent obesity in children aged 12 to 18 years old
prompt: What is the effect of combined dietary and physical activity interventions (school-based, community-based or family-based programmes with both a diet and a physical activity component), compared with a control condition (no intervention, usual curriculum or usual care), on body mass index (BMI) in adolescents aged about 12 to 18 years, measured at short-term follow-up?  Effect measure: pool as a mean difference (MD) in BMI (kg/m²) using a random-effects model. MD < 0 means a lower BMI with the intervention (favours the intervention). Orient every estimate as intervention minus control.  Outcome: BMI in kg/m² (not z-scores or percentiles) at the first assessment after the intervention ended, up to 12 months after the intervention finished. - Prefer the between-group difference the trial reports (adjusted or unadjusted, with a standard error, confidence interval or p-value). Take the SE from the confidence interval (width ÷ 3.92) or from the p-value and sample size, and state how you derived it. - If no between-group difference is reported, use the end-of-follow-up mean, SD and number for each group, or the mean change from baseline and its SD for each group, and compute the difference. - If the number analysed per arm is not stated for BMI, use the number randomised or enrolled per arm and say so. Do not leave group sizes blank. - If a paper reports only model-predicted or adjusted means per arm without a direct difference, subtract them (intervention minus control); if no SE can be derived, leave the trial out and say so. - Accept trials whose age range overlaps 12 to 18 years (for example 10 to 18, or school grades 7 to 12) when most participants are adolescents. - If a trial reports several short-term time points, use the first after the end of the intervention. Do not use medium- or long-term follow-up (beyond 12 months after the intervention). - If a trial has several intervention arms, combine those with both diet and activity components into one group, or use the main intervention arm, and use the control group once. - Include randomised and non-randomised controlled studies with a concurrent control group. Exclude trials with no control group, and trials of diet-only or activity-only interventions.  Do not pool BMI z-scores, BMI percentiles, waist circumference, body fat, dietary intake, physical activity levels or any other outcome.

title: Cognitive behavioural therapy added to standard care for firstepisode and recent-onset psychosis
prompt: In people with first-episode or recent-onset psychosis, what is the effect of adding CBT to standard care (vs. standard care alone or another psychosocial intervention plus standard care) on negative symptoms of schizophrenia (e.g., PANSS-negative or SANS score)? Use one endpoint per study, preferring the medium-term (≤12 months) assessment. Evaluate ONLY negative symptoms — no other outcome.

title: Immune checkpoint inhibitors plus platinum-based chemotherapy compared to platinum-based chemotherapy with or without bevacizumab for first-line treatment of older people with advanced non-small cell lung cancer
prompt: What is the effect of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) plus platinum-based chemotherapy, compared with chemotherapy alone (with or without placebo), on overall survival at any time point, specifically in people aged 65 years and older? Do not restrict to a narrower age band (e.g. 65 to a specific upper age) — that is a separate, related analysis in this review. Extract the Hazard Ratio directly from each trial's own survival analysis (log[HR] + SE, or HR with 95% CI).

title: Resistance training for fatigue in people with cancer
prompt:
What is the effect of resistance training during anticancer therapy, compared with no
training, on cancer-related fatigue measured at 12 weeks or less, in people with cancer?
Fatigue is a lower-is-better outcome (a higher score means more fatigue). Pool as a
standardized mean difference, since different studies use different fatigue instruments.
Do not include fatigue measured at later follow-up windows (>12 weeks) — those are separate
outcomes in this review.

title: Sodium-glucose co-transporter protein 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors for people with chronic kidney disease and diabetes
prompt:
What is the effect of sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin, bexagliflozin or similar), compared with placebo, on non-fatal myocardial infarction in adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (all stages of kidney disease, including people with preserved kidney function in the trial population)?

Effect measure: pool as a hazard ratio (HR) from the reported hazard ratio and 95% confidence interval, using a random-effects model on the log hazard ratio. HR < 1 means fewer non-fatal myocardial infarctions with the SGLT2 inhibitor (favours the SGLT2 inhibitor).

Outcome: the time-to-first-event hazard ratio for non-fatal myocardial infarction, SGLT2 inhibitor versus placebo, with its 95% confidence interval.
- Use the hazard ratio the paper reports for non-fatal (not fatal and non-fatal combined) myocardial infarction, from the main results text, a results table, the figure of secondary or exploratory outcomes, or the supplementary results table in the PDF. Convert the confidence interval to a standard error of the log HR.
- Do not rebuild a hazard ratio from event counts. If a paper reports non-fatal MI only as counts, leave it out of this analysis and say so.
- If a trial reports hazard ratios for several populations (for example the whole trial population and a chronic kidney disease subgroup), use the whole randomised population.
- Orient the HR as SGLT2 inhibitor versus placebo, and invert it (HR to 1/HR, with the interval swapped) if the paper reports placebo versus SGLT2 inhibitor.
- If a trial has several SGLT2 inhibitor doses, use the combined-dose hazard ratio the paper reports, or the pooled treatment arm versus placebo.
- Use the longest follow-up reported.
- Include only randomised placebo-controlled trials of an SGLT2 inhibitor in adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, or cardiovascular outcome trials whose population included people with chronic kidney disease. Exclude trials against an active comparator and trials of other drug classes.

Do not pool fatal myocardial infarction, any myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death, heart failure, kidney outcomes or adverse events.

title: Digital health, technology-driven or technology-assisted interventions for the management of obesity in children and adolescents
prompt: What is the effect of digital health, technology-driven or technology-assisted interventions combined with conventional care, compared with conventional care alone, on waist circumference (cm) at the end of the study in children and adolescents (aged 0 to 19 years) with overweight or obesity?
